b1-w1-new-q11-11.html:
From 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health. In the delayed degenerative disease stage CVD and cancer are the leading causes of death; prevention delays onset and treatment prolongs survival, life expectancy reaches about 70+, and age-related disease such as Alzheimer's rises (high-income countries).

  • A fails: pestilence and famine is malnutrition and infection, with CVD only 5-10% of deaths.
  • B fails: in receding pandemics people do live long enough (to about 50) to experience chronic disease.
  • C: the lecture describes this stage as chronic disease overtaking infection with CVD at under 50% of deaths - see the flag.

flags.title: Option C also matches the lecture
flags.html: 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health gives the degenerative and man-made disease stage as chronic conditions overtaking infection with CVD at “< 50%” of deaths, and 02 - Tasks of a Physician 1 says the same. That is what option C states, so on the notes C is not clearly false. D is the stage the notes describe unambiguously.

b1-w1-new-q16-16:
From 10 - Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees.

  • A true: the lecture organizes refugee health issues into pre-migration (trauma, violence), migration (dangerous journey, camps, family separation) and post-migration stages.
  • B true: post-migration issues include securing housing and financial stability and difficult access to services.
  • D true: children without parents or a guardian are especially vulnerable (a WHO point).
  • C false: mental health (PTSD, repeated losses) and chronic disease (untreated through health-system breakdown or a long journey) are two of the WHO's five areas of refugee health.

b1-w1-new-q17-17.html: From 10 - Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees. The lecture's cultural competence continuum places forced assimilation and subjugation (cultural destructiveness) and racism (cultural incapacity) at its lowest stages, and grounds cultural safety in self-determination and decolonization - a concept first defined because of poor health outcomes in the colonized Maori people. Colonization is the historical system and racism the ongoing practice that sustains it, so they act together on Indigenous health, which is why decolonizing care is offered as the remedy.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: No lecture note addresses Indigenous health in Canada directly; the reasoning extends the cultural safety and decolonization material in 10 - Cultural Competence. Verify it before relying on it.

b1-w1-new-q2-2:
From 01 - Introduction to MCC Clinical Presentations. A symptom is what the patient perceives as not normal and complains of; a sign is objective evidence the practitioner observes or elicits on examination. A severe rash is both: the patient notices it and comes in because of it, and the clinician can see and describe it.

  • A or B alone is incomplete - each captures only one side of the finding.
  • D fails: a diagnosis identifies the underlying illness (burn, poisoning); “rash” is a finding that still needs a differential.
b1-w1-new-q3-3:
From 02 - Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach. The patient-centred method splits context in two. Proximal context is generally modifiable and directly influences illness: family, education, employment, social supports, financial security. Distal context is non-modifiable and acts indirectly: culture, community, faith/beliefs, ecosystem, society.

  • A (faith/beliefs), C (culture) and D (society) are all distal.
  • E fails because it pairs a distal factor (faith) with employment.

b1-w1-new-q6-6.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization (Week 2), which holds the imaging material. The question asks for the false statement. The lecture's density table runs air (black) → water (charcoal) → soft tissue (grey) → bone (white) → metal (white with beam hardening), so bone appearing grey is false.

  • A true: radiographs separate structures by tissue opacity (silhouetting), which follows density.
  • B true: MRI weighting (T1 for fat, T2 for fluid, proton density for cartilage and tendon) distinguishes soft tissues x-ray cannot.
  • C true: ultrasound uses high-frequency sound in real time; the Doppler detail is not in the note but is standard.

b1-w2-meds2024-q12-12:
From 08 - Cellular Communication. In the lecture's sequence, after the peak at about +45 mV the V.G. K+ channels, which are slower than the Na+ channels, keep opening while the V.G. Na+ channels become inactivated; K+ rushes out and the membrane repolarizes from +45 back toward -70 mV.

  • Depolarization is driven by rapid Na+ channel opening and Na+ influx.
  • Hyperpolarization is the undershoot while K+ channels close slowly and K+ keeps leaving.
  • Resting membrane potential is set by K+ leak channels and the Na+/K+ pump, with V.G. channels in their resting configuration.

b1-w2-meds2024-q14-14.html:
From 02 - Genetics (Week 3), with prions from 16 - How Viruses Work. A dominant negative effect is a mutant protein that disrupts the normal protein from the other allele, usually by interacting with it - “better to have no neighbour than a bad one”.

  • i fits: the lecture's own example is severe osteogenesis imperfecta, where the mutated alpha chain is incorporated and ruins orderly collagen coiling.
  • iii fits by the same logic: a prion is a misfolded protein that transmits its misfolded shape onto normal copies of the same protein.
  • ii fails: the CFTR defect in cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive loss of function - carriers are fine because the normal copy is a backup, so nothing is poisoning it.

flags.title: Numbering lost from the stem
flags.html: The roman numerals in this question were stripped when it was transcribed; the three scenarios are i (collagen), ii (CFTR), iii (prions) in the order the stem lists them.

b1-w2-meds2024-q3-3:
From 05 - Muscle Tissue. The question asks for the incorrect statement. The lecture's table has skeletal and cardiac muscle as striated; only smooth muscle is not, so C is wrong.

  • A correct: cardiac and smooth muscle each have a single central nucleus (skeletal is a multinucleated syncytium with peripheral nuclei).
  • B correct: skeletal is voluntary; cardiac and smooth are involuntary.
  • D correct: T-tubules are in skeletal (triads) and cardiac (wider, at the Z line, diads); smooth muscle uses caveolae instead.
  • E correct: intercalated discs (gap junctions, adherens junctions, desmosomes) are unique to cardiac muscle.
b1-w2-meds2024-q4-4:
From 05 - Muscle Tissue. The A band is the length of the thick (myosin) filaments, which stay stationary; in the sliding filament model the thin filaments slide over them, so filament lengths do not change and the A band stays constant.

  • H zone shortens: it is the thick-filament-only centre, which narrows as thin filaments slide in.
  • I band shortens: it is the thin-filament-only region, which narrows as the Z lines are pulled toward the M line.
  • U band is not a sarcomere structure (the bands are A, I, H, with Z and M lines).
b1-w2-meds2024-q6-6:
From 07 - Nerves. Oligodendrocytes myelinate axons in the central nervous system, one cell covering many axons (40-50 internodal segments); the lecture names CNS demyelination as multiple sclerosis, and because oligodendrocytes do not proliferate there is no repair.

  • C fails: myelinated PNS axons are wrapped by Schwann cells, one cell per segment of one axon - these are spared in MS.
  • A and B fail: unmyelinated axons have no myelin for an attack on myelinating cells to remove.
b1-w2-new-q10-10:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. The four bone cells form a lineage plus one outsider.

  • A marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells = osteoprogenitor cells (III), in the periosteum and endosteum, which differentiate into osteoblasts during repair.
  • B actively secrete matrix = osteoblasts (II), which also start mineralization with alkaline phosphatase.
  • C interconnected network that maintains calcification = osteocytes (IV): osteoblasts walled into matrix, linked by canaliculi, and mechanosensory.
  • D multinucleated cells that resorb matrix = osteoclasts (I), the outsider, fused from blood monocytes/macrophages rather than the mesenchymal line.

b1-w2-new-q13-13.html:
From 07 - Nerves. The lecture defines Nissl bodies as stacks of endoplasmic reticulum: rough ER studded with ribosomes, in the neuron's cell body (perikaryon). The heavy protein synthesis they carry out supplies the long axon. The answer the lecture supports is C.

  • B (groups of Golgi bodies) is not what Nissl bodies are. The lecture's only Golgi point is that the Golgi apparatus is not found in axons.
  • A (mitochondria) and D (peroxisomes) are other organelles, not the basophilic clumps that make up Nissl substance.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key is B (groups of Golgi bodies), but 07 - Nerves states “Nissl bodies = stacks of endoplasmic reticulum”, which is option C.

b1-w2-new-q16-16.html:
From 02 - Physiology (Homeostasis). The note's discriminator: a negative feedback loop counteracts the stimulus and is homeostatic, while a positive loop reinforces the stimulus and needs an external event to stop it.

  • C (childbirth): contractions push the fetus against the cervix, which drives stronger contractions; the loop only ends with delivery.
  • E (blood clotting): each activated factor recruits more, amplifying the clot until the vessel is sealed.
  • A, B, D (temperature, blood sugar, osmolality) are the note's own examples of monitored variables held in an acceptable range: a deviation triggers a correction that shuts itself off, which is negative feedback.

flags.title: Partly beyond the note
flags.html: 02 - Physiology (Homeostasis) defines positive and negative feedback but does not name childbirth or clotting as examples; those two are reasoned from the definition. Verify before relying on it.

b1-w2-new-q18-18:
From 02 - Osmosis. Tonicity is a solution's ability to cause water movement. A hypotonic solution (about 200 mOsm/kg against the cell's ~300) has less solute outside than inside, so water is drawn into the cell by osmosis and it swells (the note's mnemonic: the ‘O’ in hypOtonic means the cell expands).

  • A (no change) describes an isotonic solution, where there is no net water movement.
  • B (shrink) describes a hypertonic solution, which pulls water out of the cell.
b1-w2-new-q19-19:
From 08 - Cellular Communication. The note's sequence: a graded depolarization reaches threshold (about −55 mV); voltage-gated Na+ channels open and the membrane depolarizes rapidly to about +45 mV; Na+ channels inactivate and K+ rushes out, repolarizing it toward −70 mV; the slow K+ channels stay open too long, so it hyperpolarizes (undershoot) before the Na+/K+ pump restores rest.

  • A puts repolarization before depolarization; there is nothing to repolarize from yet.
  • C starts with repolarization and ends with depolarization, the reverse of the cycle.
  • D swaps the last two: the undershoot follows repolarization, it does not precede it.
b1-w2-new-q2-2:
From 01 - Biochemistry. The note states that the main function of enzymes is to lower activation energy. They do not supply it, so A is the false statement.

  • B is true word for word: enzymes facilitate a reaction that could happen on its own but does not, or happens very slowly.
  • C is true: a catalyst speeds a reaction without changing what goes in or what comes out.
  • D is true on the note: higher substrate concentration means faster product formation, which is why a disease with little (or poorly binding) enzyme can be treated by raising the substrate to make use of the enzyme that is present.
b1-w2-new-q23-23:
From 09 - Anatomy. The note pairs dorsiflexion (bringing the toes toward the shin) with plantar flexion (pointing the toes), so pointing the toes down is plantarflexion.

  • A (depression) moves the scapulae (shoulders) away from the ears.
  • B (pronation) is a forearm movement: palms face backward with the radius and ulna crossed.
  • D (flexion) is the general term for decreasing a joint angle; at the ankle the specific terms are dorsiflexion and plantar flexion, so it is not the best answer.

b1-w2-new-q25-25.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization. The note's endocrine row lists the adrenals as regulating metabolism, the immune system, blood pressure and the stress response, and gives blood calcium to the parathyroids (and the thyroid). So D is the false pairing.

  • A is true: the pancreas is listed for blood sugar.
  • B is true: the gonads are listed for the reproductive organs and secondary sex characteristics.
  • C is true: the pineal gland is listed for circadian rhythms.

b1-w2-new-q27-27.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization. The note's CT entry: x-ray based thin axial slices, more expensive than plain radiography, with a much larger dose of ionizing radiation, and not recommended in pregnancy. That makes A true.

  • B fails on “unlike an MRI”: 09 - Anatomy says all axial scans are read as if standing at the patient's feet looking toward the head, and that convention applies to axial MRI as well.
  • C is the reverse: CT gives a much larger radiation dose than a radiograph (MRI and ultrasound use none).
  • D contradicts the note, which says CT is not recommended for pregnant women.

b1-w2-new-q7-7.html:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. Taking the terms as I loose, II dense irregular, III reticular, IV dense regular (the order the stem lists them), the keyed mapping matches the note's table exactly.

  • A – II: dense irregular CT is found in most organ capsules and the reticular layer of the dermis; its type I and III collagen is woven into a mat, making it resilient and protective.
  • B – IV: dense regular CT (tendons, ligaments, joint capsules) has fibroblasts and type I collagen in rows, for high stress resistance.
  • C – III: reticular CT (type III collagen from reticular cells) supports the hematopoietic tissues: marrow, lymph nodes, spleen.
  • D – I: loose CT sits under epithelia, carries vessels and nerves, and has poorly organized fibres.

flags.title: Numbering lost from the stem
flags.html: The roman numerals in this question were stripped when it was transcribed; the mapping assumes the four tissues are I-IV in the order the stem lists them.

b1-w2-new-q8-8.html:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. With I = white and II = brown adipose tissue:

  • White (C, D, G, H): the adult energy store and insulator; unilocular (one lipid vacuole per cell), which pushes the nucleus to the periphery; the cells can grow about 4× before dividing, and once divided are hard to clear.
  • Brown (A, B, E, F): abundant in newborns (2-5% of body weight) for thermoregulation; multilocular (many small droplets), so the nucleus stays central; packed with mitochondria, which is what makes it a heat generator.

The discriminator is locularity: one droplet displaces the nucleus, many droplets leave it central.

flags.title: Numbering lost from the stem
flags.html: The roman numerals in this question were stripped when it was transcribed; the mapping assumes I = white and II = brown adipose tissue, the order the stem lists them.

b1-w2-new-q9-9.html:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. With I hyaline, II elastic, III fibrocartilage, the key matches the note's cartilage table.

  • A – II: elastic cartilage (type II collagen plus elastin) is where shape must spring back: epiglottis, larynx, pinna and auditory canal.
  • B – III: fibrocartilage (types I and II collagen, chondrocytes in parallel rows) resists compression: intervertebral discs, menisci, the jaw, tendon insertions.
  • C – I: hyaline, the most common type (type II collagen, isogenous groups), forms the growth plates, ventral rib ends and the walls of the respiratory tree.

flags.title: Numbering lost from the stem
flags.html: The roman numerals in this question were stripped when it was transcribed; the mapping assumes I = hyaline, II = elastic, III = fibrocartilage, the order the stem lists them.

b1-w2-sa-q13-13:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. The note describes the osteoclast as formed by the fusion of peripheral blood monocytes/macrophages, multinucleated (up to 30 nuclei), secreting acid and metalloproteinases that resorb bone in Howship's lacunae. Every element of C is there.

  • A describes the osteoblast, which becomes an osteocyte once enclosed in matrix.
  • B describes the osteoprogenitor cell, which differentiates into bone-depositing osteoblasts.
  • D mixes the osteoclast's nuclei with the osteocyte's location; osteocytes are single cells in lacunae derived from osteoblasts.
  • E has the right function but the wrong origin: osteoclasts come from the monocyte line, not from osteoblasts.
b1-w2-sa-q21-21:
From 01 - Biochemistry. The note says proteins are made of 20 or 21 amino acids, and lists amino acids among the essential micromolecules that combine to form macromolecules.

  • B (monosaccharides) build carbohydrates such as glycogen and starch.
  • C (nucleotides) build the nucleic acids DNA and RNA.
  • D (peptides) are short chains of amino acids, already assembled; they are a stage of protein structure, not the basic unit.
  • E (fatty acids) are the simplest lipids, stored as triglycerides.
b1-w2-sa-q22-22:
From 01 - Biochemistry. The note calls nucleic acids the “blueprint” for how to build a cell: DNA and RNA carry the genetic code in three-letter codons, and it is the nucleic acid that is isolated and sequenced (whole genome, exome or targeted panel) to read genetic information.

  • A (lipids) store energy, form membranes and act in signalling.
  • C (carbohydrates) provide energy and structural polysaccharides.
  • D (proteins) are the product the code specifies; analysing them shows what is expressed, not the inherited sequence itself.
b1-w3-new-q16-16: From 09 - Nutrition. The lecture's list of barriers to healthy food choices contains each of A-D almost word for word: financial uncertainty and the cost of healthy foods, lack of time, the need to ration food within the family, and a lack of nutrition knowledge and skills. It also adds distance from healthy food and a lack of transportation. Since every option is on the list, E (all of the above) is the only complete answer.
b1-w3-new-q18-18:
From 10 - Infant Nutrition. The lecture's special formulas are exactly these four, so E is right, while noting that most infants never need one and switching does not help colic:

  • Lactose-free: a cow's milk based formula without lactose.
  • Hydrolyzed whey: lower osmolality, may improve gastric emptying.
  • Soy: for vegetarian families, lactase deficiency and galactosemia.
  • Protein hydrolysate: for infants who cannot digest, or are allergic to, intact protein, or with fat malabsorption; more expensive.
b1-w3-new-q7-7:
From 02 - Genetics. Affected individuals are almost all male, and the pattern follows the X. The affected mother (1) has both sons affected and her daughters (4, 6) unaffected, which fits carrier daughters. Carrier daughter 4 with an unaffected partner has one affected son (9), and all her daughters are unaffected: the note's “female carriers to sons”. Affected son 7 married to an affected woman (8) has all children affected, as expected when the mother has two variant X's.

  • A (AD) fails because unaffected 4 has an affected son (a skipped generation).
  • B (AR) would need unrelated partners 2 and 3 both to be carriers, and would not favour males.
  • D (new dominant) fails because the grandmother is already affected, so nothing arose de novo.

The figure is printed mirror-reversed, so the numbers read backwards.
b1-w3-ra-q1-1:
From 02 - Genetics. The mother had ADPKD, an autosomal dominant condition, and the note gives the rule: a 1 in 2 (50%) chance that each child inherits the trait, males and females equally. Her hypertension and abdominal distension raise suspicion, but the question asks only for the inheritance-based prior risk.

  • A (1%) is the gonadal-mosaicism recurrence risk after a de novo mutation, but here the mother is affected.
  • B (25%) applies to autosomal recessive inheritance from two carrier parents.
  • D (75%) would need both parents affected.
b1-w3-ra-q4-4:
From 02 - Genetics. The note names Duchenne muscular dystrophy as its example of X-linked inheritance: males are affected almost exclusively because they are hemizygous, and the variant passes from female carriers to sons. That is exactly this family, a carrier mother with an affected son.

  • B (AD) would make the carrier mother affected herself.
  • C (mitochondrial) would give disease to all her children regardless of sex, and involves mtDNA, not a nuclear gene like DMD.
  • D (AR) would need the father to be a carrier too, and would not favour sons.
b1-w3-ra-q5-5:
From 02 - Genetics. A carrier mother has one normal and one DMD-variant X, and each child receives one of them at random. So each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the variant. The note's breakdown by sex: 50% of sons affected and 50% of daughters carriers.

  • A fails because daughters also get their father's normal X, so they are at most carriers (unless skewed X inactivation), not all affected.
  • B overstates it: half of daughters are carriers, not all. “All daughters carriers” is the rule for an affected father.
  • C overstates it: half of sons, not all.

b1-w3-sa-q5-5.html:
From 07 - Chromosome Disorder Testing. The lecture's organising idea: a karyotype shows chromosome structure, including balanced rearrangements, while a microarray shows gene content, that is, gains and losses. A balanced translocation such as t(11;22) moves material without adding or removing any (06 - Chromosomal Anomalies: “no missing information, but the information is shuffled”), so a microarray sees a normal dosage. It needs a karyotype.

  • A (Turner, 45,X) is a whole-chromosome loss, an obvious dosage change.
  • B (15q11.2 deletion) and E (500 kb DMD duplication) are submicroscopic copy-number changes, the imbalances microarray exists to find.
  • D (mosaic trisomy 21) is extra chromosome 21 material in a proportion of cells, still a gain in content.

flags.title: Partly beyond the note
flags.html: 07 - Chromosome Disorder Testing does not address mosaicism; that microarray can detect mosaic trisomy (at a reasonable mosaic level) is reasoned from its detecting gains in content.

b1-w4-new-q16-16:
From 04 - School Age. Piaget's stages in the note's order: sensorimotor (0-2) – learning through activity, object permanence; preoperational (2-7) – symbolic representation and play; concrete operational (7-11) – conservation, reversibility, classifying by more than one quality; formal operational (12+) – abstract and hypothetical reasoning (C).

  • A and D start with preoperational, but object permanence and sensorimotor learning come first.
  • B puts formal before concrete; logical thought about concrete objects precedes abstract thought.
b1-w4-new-q7-7:
From 07 - The Child with a (Dis)Ability. The note's six steps for giving the news of a disability are: introduce self, sit down if parents are agreeable, give a warning phrase, get to the point quickly, allow parents time to absorb the information, and be comfortable with silence and remain present. All four options are on that list.

“Get to the point quickly” is the one students hesitate over. It sits alongside the warning phrase, not against empathy: once warned, parents are served by directness rather than a long lead-in. Around the conversation, the informing interview has a familiar provider, both parents present, a timely diagnosis, and follow-up time to review.
b1-w4-sa-q11-11:
From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. The note's live attenuated viral vaccines are measles, oral polio, rotavirus, varicella and yellow fever, and live vaccines are contraindicated in the immunocompromised, pregnant women and neonates because they can cause vaccine-strain disease (C). Every other option is non-live:

  • A (Hib) is a conjugate subunit vaccine.
  • B (pneumococcal polysaccharide) is a polysaccharide subunit vaccine (poorly immunogenic under 2 years).
  • D (hepatitis B) is a protein subunit vaccine.
  • E (hepatitis A) is an inactivated whole-cell vaccine.

b1-w4-sa-q4-4.html:
From 06 - Adolescent Development. Every listed option is a recognised consequence of restrictive dieting, so “all of the above” (E):

  • A – energy restriction suppresses the reproductive axis, giving menstrual irregularity or amenorrhea.
  • B – undernutrition causes poor concentration, irritability and fatigue.
  • C – restriction drives a restrict-binge cycle.
  • D – dieting is a leading risk factor for developing an eating disorder.

The note's approach reflects this seriousness: ask how long the teen has been changing their eating to influence shape or weight, take lying and standing vitals, an ECG, and a broad panel of bloodwork.

flags.title: Mostly beyond the note
flags.html: 06 - Adolescent Development gives only the screening question and the work-up for disordered eating; the listed consequences of dieting are from general principles. Verify them before relying on them.

b1-w1-new-q18-18.html:
All four are colonial policies and practices whose effects on Indigenous health persist, so E.

  • A: the Indian Act (1876) imposed federal control over First Nations identity, governance and land, and is still in force.
  • B: forced relocation of Inuit communities (the High Arctic relocations of the 1950s) broke ties to land and livelihood.
  • C: the residential school system removed children from families and culture, with abuse and intergenerational trauma.
  • D: child welfare, past (the Sixties Scoop) and present (overrepresentation of Indigenous children in care), continues that separation.

The course's cultural safety material ties this together: cultural safety rests on self-determination and de-colonization.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

b1-w1-new-q8-8.html:
Chronic stress keeps the arousal system (sympathetic and HPA axis) switched on. That sustained activation is itself a source of long-term biological damage (A), and chronic cortisol exposure promotes appetite, central fat deposition and weight gain (C). So the key is D, “A and C”, and it rules out B.

The bank's reason for excluding B is that ADH is not produced during stress. That is questionable (see the flag). A safer reading is that B is wrong as a blanket “high levels of ADH and cortisol” claim, so E (“all of the above”) falls with it.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

flags.title: The bank's rationale is doubtful
flags.html: The source key says ADH is not produced during stress. In standard physiology, vasopressin (ADH) is co-secreted with CRH during stress and potentiates ACTH release, so stress can raise ADH. The keyed letter (D) may still reflect the course's intent, but do not learn “stress does not release ADH” from this question. No note covers it.

b1-wb-fom-q8.html:
From 02 - Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach. VITAMIN C&D classifies by cause, and the cause here is a motorcycle striking him: the T of VITAMIN, traumatic/toxic (C). The bruising and internal bleeding are the result, not the category.

  • A (vascular) is the tempting distractor, since bleeding involves vessels, but vascular means a primary vessel problem such as an aneurysm or infarct, not a vessel torn by impact.
  • B, D, E: nothing infectious, autoimmune or metabolic is suggested.
  • F, G, H, I: no medical intervention, tumour, congenital lesion or degeneration explains an acute injury after a collision.

review.t: Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach

b1-wb-fom-q86.html:
From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation (Block 2) and 02 - Imaging in Cardiovascular Disease (PoM 1). The Framingham risk score estimates 10-year cardiovascular disease risk from age, sex, smoking status, total cholesterol, HDL and systolic BP (D). It drives lipid management: under 10% lifestyle and re-estimate in 5 years, 10-19% add a moderate-potency statin, 20% or more a high-potency statin.

  • A: osteoporosis risk is estimated with other tools (such as FRAX).
  • B: diabetes risk has its own calculators; diabetes is an input to CV risk, not Framingham's output.
  • C: it is a clinical CVD risk tool, not an actuarial life-expectancy table.

b1-w2-meds2024-q10-10.html:
From 05 - Muscle Tissue. The sequence in the note: Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin C, causing a conformational change that frees tropomyosin from the myosin-binding sites on actin. Myosin then binds actin and makes its power stroke. So calcium-bound troponin lets tropomyosin come away from actin (C).

  • A reverses the effect: calcium-bound troponin permits actin-myosin binding.
  • B names the wrong calcium-binding protein: calcium binds troponin, not tropomyosin.
  • D: calcium does not bind the actin-myosin complex; the power stroke is the myosin head's conformational change.
  • E: calcium does not act through myosin here, and the effect is to move tropomyosin away from actin, not bind it on.

b1-w2-meds2024-q11-11.html:
From 08 - Cellular Communication. The note's modes of cell signalling are autocrine (a cell signals itself), paracrine (short-distance messengers), cell-cell contact (mediators through gap junctions), synaptic (neurotransmitter release) and endocrine (hormones carried in the bloodstream).

  • A (synaptic), B (gap junctions), C (endocrine) and D (paracrine) are all on that list.
  • E (“uterine”) names an organ, not a signalling mode, so it is the exception. The uterus's own cells communicate through the modes above; visceral smooth muscle there uses gap junctions.

b1-w2-new-q22-22.html:
From 05 - Muscle Tissue. Excitation-contraction coupling runs electrical → chemical → mechanical:

  • The action potential spreads down the T-tubules (inward folds of the sarcolemma).
  • This makes the sarcoplasmic reticulum release Ca2+ from its terminal cisternae (the triad).
  • Ca2+ binds troponin C, shifting tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites.
  • Only then can myosin bind actin and perform the power stroke, so actin slides over myosin and the I band and H zone shorten.

A puts myosin binding before calcium-troponin binding, impossible while tropomyosin blocks the sites. B and D release calcium before the voltage reaches the SR, reversing cause and effect.

b1-w2-new-q26-26.html:
From 07 - Nerves and 10 - Body System Organization. Sensory neurons are pseudo-unipolar or bipolar cells that carry impulses from receptors to the CNS: they are the afferent fibres, so D is true. Motor neurons are the efferent limb.

  • A false: the peripheral nervous system has 12 pairs of cranial nerves.
  • B false: there are 31 pairs of spinal nerves.
  • C false: voluntary movement is skeletal muscle under somatic motor control; the sympathetic system is part of the autonomic, involuntary division.

b1-w2-new-q28-28.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization. The lecture's radiograph rules answer every option. A structure needs a minimum of 2 radiographs at 90° to one another (e.g. AP/PA plus lateral), because one 2D view suffers from summation, where overlapping structures mimic an abnormality. Four is not the minimum, so C is the false statement.

  • A true: plain films use ionizing radiation, but CT is the modality the lecture singles out for a much larger dose.
  • B true: a radiograph is a 2D projection, unlike CT's slices.
  • D true: air is least dense and appears black; bone and metal appear white.

b1-w2-new-q3-3.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization. Each level of blinding hides allocation from one more party (stem order: I open label, II single, III double, IV triple):

  • Open label (I) = all parties aware → B.
  • Single blind (II) = the patient or the clinician is unaware → D.
  • Double blind (III) = both patient and investigator unaware → A.
  • Triple blind (IV) = patient, investigator and the analysts unaware → C.

12 - Evidence-Based Medicine adds why it matters: blinding reduces performance and detection bias, and is critical when the outcome is subjective, less so when it is objective.

b1-wb-fom-q78.html:
From 03 - Body Systems Integration (Week 5). All venous blood leaving the GI tract enters the portal system, draining through the portal vein to the liver before it reaches the systemic veins: absorbed nutrients → portal system → liver → caval system → IVC → right atrium.

  • C hepatic veins come after the liver, carrying blood out of it into the IVC.
  • A IVC is later still: it receives the hepatic veins.
  • D SVC drains the head, neck and upper limbs, not the gut.

The first-pass route through the liver is why the order matters.

b1-w3-new-q13-13.html:
From 01 - Child Development and 08 - Developmental Milestones. The Nipissing (LookSee) checklist is a parent-completed questionnaire of yes/no questions about what the child can do, reviewed by the physician. One “no” is a positive screen, and it is very sensitive but not very specific. It is used repeatedly at well-child visits across early childhood (Nipissing Plus adds photos for less literate parents).

  • A true: short yes/no list about abilities.
  • B true: it tracks development over the early years at each visit.
  • C false: it is a screening tool; a positive screen leads to assessment, and only assessment diagnoses.

So D (A and B).

flags.title: Option B is only partly covered
flags.html: The notes describe the Nipissing as a repeated parent questionnaire but do not give its age range; “1 month to 6 years” is taken from the question, not the lecture.

b1-w3-new-q9-9.html:
From 05 - Genetic Screening, as far as it goes. The lecture says Down syndrome risk rises with maternal age, uses 1:350 as the eFTS cut-off, and funds NIPT from age 40. The usual age-related figures run roughly 1:350 at 35, rising to about 1:175 around 38 and 1:100 at 40, so a 38-year-old sits between 1:175 and 1:100 (C).

  • A 1:900-1:600 is the risk of women around 30 or younger.
  • B 1:350-1:175 covers 35-37.
  • D greater than 1:100 applies from about 40 onward.

The logic to remember: the risk roughly doubles every 2-3 years after 35.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

b1-w3-ra-q2-2.html:
From 07 - Chromosome Disorder Testing. Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY: an extra X in a male, giving tall stature, gynecomastia, small testes, learning disability and infertility with a normal appearance. The other options are the other syndromes in the lecture's table:

  • A 45,X = Turner syndrome (webbed neck, coarctation, short stature, primary amenorrhea).
  • C trisomy 13 = Patau (midline defects, cleft palate, polydactyly).
  • D trisomy 18 = Edward (rocker-bottom feet, overlapping fingers, cardiac defects).

B is the intended answer only if it reads 47,XXY.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The keyed option B reads “47, XX”, but 07 - Chromosome Disorder Testing and 07 - The Child with a (Dis)Ability (Week 4) both give Klinefelter as 47,XXY. The Y was probably dropped in transcription; as written, no option is correct.

b1-w3-ra-q3-3.html:
From 02 - Genetics. Autosomal recessive disorders need two variant alleles: affected children usually appear in one sibship of one generation with unaffected carrier parents, males and females equally, and consanguinity raises the chance. The lecture gives cystic fibrosis (CFTR, ΔF508) as the classic example, so A.

  • B Patau syndrome is trisomy 13, a numerical chromosome abnormality (aneuploidy), not a single-gene disorder.
  • C Turner syndrome is 45,X, a monosomy.
  • D Down syndrome is trisomy 21, usually from nondisjunction in meiosis I.

The discriminator: Mendelian inheritance patterns describe single genes; the three distractors are whole-chromosome errors.

b1-w3-sa-q16-16.html:
From 10 - Infant Nutrition. The lecture recommends that babies are breastfed exclusively until 6 months of age, with breastfeeding continued up to 2 years. Term infants have adequate iron stores from the mother up to 6 months, which is why iron-rich solids are added only after that. Breastfed infants need vitamin D 400 IU/day (01 - Child Development).

  • B cow's milk is not an infant diet in the first 6 months.
  • C, D formula is an alternative when breastfeeding is not possible, not the recommendation; iron is also less well absorbed from formula.
  • E rice cereal is a solid food, introduced from about 6 months.

b1-w3-sa-q4-4.html:
From 05 - Genetic Screening. Newborn screening detects babies at risk; it is NOT diagnostic, and screens carry false positives. A positive result therefore means clinical assessment plus definitive testing before anyone is labelled affected.

  • B wrong: a positive screen raises the probability; it is never dismissed because the disease is rare.
  • C wrong: one variant in a recessive gene usually means a carrier, but 02 - Genetics notes that two variants on different alleles (trans) cause disease, a second variant can be missed, and not every panel disorder is recessive.
  • D wrong: it treats a screen as a diagnosis.
  • E wrong: disorders are chosen by the Wilson and Jungner criteria (serious, asymptomatic stage, treatable), not by Ontario prevalence.

b1-w3-sa-q7-7.html:
From 08 - Developmental Milestones. Check each finding against the 18-month row and the red flags:

  • C concerning: poor eye contact is an early sign of autism spectrum disorder (with ritualistic behaviour and little symbolic play), and lack of eye contact and engagement is a listed red flag. Social-communication signs predict outcome more than motor ones.
  • A normal: 18 months expects 6-20 single words with meaning; 12 is in range. The red flag is no single words by 18 months.
  • B normal: 18 months is “walks well”; running comes at 24 months. Not walking at 18 months would be the flag.
  • D normal: temper tantrums and high activity are expected from 18 to 36 months.

b1-w4-ra-q4-4.html:
From 06 - Adolescent Development and 07 - The Child with a (Dis)Ability. She has just reached menarche with little sex education, so the first visit starts from normal puberty and sexual development: the 7 Ps of sexual health and her developing identity apply to her as to any adolescent. The disability lecture warns against assuming a patient with a disability cannot make her own decisions, and the adolescent lecture lists family planning among the adult tasks to prepare for.

  • B, E her recurrence risk and folic acid (05 - Genetic Screening) matter for later preconception counselling, not as the first focus.
  • C telling her people with disabilities should not have children is discriminatory and false.
  • D brushing off her questions leaves her without knowledge she needs now.

b1-w4-sa-q12-12.html:
From 08 - Developmental Milestones. At 24 months the lecture expects running, climbing stairs, 50+ words, 2-word phrases, and imaginative play close to an adult. Checking the options against the table:

  • A hopping on one foot = 60 months (standing on one foot briefly is 36).
  • B riding a tricycle is a 3-year skill; at 30 months the lecture lists only a push car.
  • C using pronouns = 36 months (“asks questions, uses pronouns”).
  • D jumping on two feet is listed at 30 months, the nearest to 2 years, so it is the best answer.
  • E cooperative play = 48 months (parallel play at 36).

flags.title: The lecture dates jumping at 30 months
flags.html: 08 - Developmental Milestones and 07 - The Child with a (Dis)Ability both place jumping on two feet at 2.5 years, not 2. D is still the closest option to 24 months, but the key's “2-year motor milestone” is half a year early on the lecture.

b2-w5-new-q10-10.html:
From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation (and 06 - Adult Screening - Diagnostic Pathway for vitals). Statement by statement:

  • i - HR, RR, temperature and BP are the classic vitals; every option includes i, so the question treats it as true (06 also lists O2 saturation).
  • ii true - systemic veins, the capacitance vessels, hold about 70% of the ~5 L blood volume.
  • iii true - biological gender is on the lecture's list of factors that affect BP.
  • iv - the lecture ties TPR to vessel diameter (larger diameter = lower resistance), and lists blood volume as a separate factor in BP. It never links TPR to blood volume.
  • v false - the PNS slows HR and contractility, so the heart has both SNS and PNS supply (the PNS just does not innervate the blood vessels).

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key (D) needs statement iv to be true, but 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation relates TPR to vessel diameter and lists blood volume as a separate determinant of BP alongside cardiac output, peripheral resistance, viscosity and vessel elasticity. On the lecture, iv is unsupported, which would make B (i, ii, iii) the answer. The key's own rationale addresses only statement v.

b2-w5-new-q12-12:
From 09 - Approach to Anxiety and Stress. The lecture's symptom-cluster tables sort each symptom into a sphere and a disorder. Avoidance (behavioural), worry (emotional) and catastrophizing (cognitive) belong to the anxiety cluster; impaired concentration and insomnia appear in both clusters, so they fit anxiety as well. Every symptom here fits anxiety.

  • A - the depression markers are missing: sadness, hopelessness, worthlessness, loss of interest, isolating, suicidal ideation.
  • B, D - there is nothing to suggest mania, or obsessions and compulsions; the lecture gives no cluster that matches this pattern better than anxiety.
b2-w5-new-q14-14:
From 10 - Approach to Abnormal Test Results. The informed-consent section opens with the point: any test can find something bad, so the patient must understand what they are undergoing and what could result, and it is ultimately up to the patient whether to proceed. Explanation and consent therefore come before anything is ordered or collected.

  • A, B - knowing the collection steps and making the requisition are logistics that follow a decision the patient has not yet made.
  • D - telling the patient and then ordering skips consent: telling is not the same as the patient agreeing voluntarily with capacity.

b2-w5-new-q20-20.html:
From 12 - Adult Screening and Preventative Care Principles. The lecture runs the inflammatory response as the 5 Rs, and the order follows the logic of the response: Recognition of the offending agent by host cells and molecules → Recruitment of leukocytes and plasma proteins from the circulation → Removal of the agent by the activated cells → Regulation, controlling and terminating the reaction → Resolution, repair of the damaged tissue.

  • A, B - cells cannot be recruited before the agent has been recognized.
  • C - nothing can remove the agent until leukocytes have been recruited.
  • E - regulation (termination) comes after removal; switching the response off first would leave the agent in place.

review.t: Adult Screening and Preventative Care Principles

b2-w5-new-q3-3:
From 06 - Adult Screening - Diagnostic Pathway (its tube-colour chart; and 07 - Introduction to Laboratory Medicine). The chart pairs the lavender (purple) K2 EDTA tube with the full blood count (FBC/CBC), along with HbA1c and ESR. 07 names collecting the proper specimen type in the correct tube, in the correct order of draw, as the basis of an accurate result; the wrong tube is a pre-analytical error.

  • A red - a clot activator, so the blood clots; the chart uses it for antibody screens and vitamin D.
  • C green - lithium heparin, for STAT biochemistry, electrolytes and renal function.
  • D navy (royal blue) - trace elements and heavy metals (zinc, copper, lead, mercury).

b2-w5-new-q5-5.html:
From 08 - Choosing Wisely Review (and 07 - Introduction to Laboratory Medicine). The lecture defines Choosing Wisely as appropriate utilization, balancing underutilization and overutilization. Rationing withholds care to save resources, which is underuse: the reverse of what the campaign is for, so B is not a reason for it.

  • A - the volume of unnecessary testing is the problem the campaign exists to address.
  • C - a reason: 07 shows predictive value falls with prevalence, so testing low-probability patients makes a positive result increasingly likely to be false.
  • D - harm is a reason: inappropriate testing leads to unnecessary procedures and treatment, and so to patient harm.

flags.title: Two of the figures are not in the notes
flags.html: The “more than 1 million” figure (A) and the claim about harm from cascades after incidental findings (D) do not appear in 08 - Choosing Wisely Review, which states only that inappropriate testing causes unnecessary procedures and patient harm. Verify them before relying on them.

b2-w5-new-q6-6.html:
From 08 - Choosing Wisely Review. The lecture's “Why Choosing Wisely?” table gives drivers of over-testing at every level, and each option is one of them:

  • A the silo effect - health systems (culture and historical practice).
  • B revenue - labs.
  • C malpractice fear - physicians, alongside patient pressure, incentives and fee for service.
  • D “more is better” - patients, alongside wellness movements and Dr. Google.

Because every stakeholder contributes, all of the above is the answer, and no single option accounts for the problem alone.

b2-w5-ra-q10-10:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The four adaptations are told apart by what changes:

  • Hypertrophy - bigger cells, no new cells; the response of skeletal and cardiac muscle (limited division) to increased workload.
  • Hyperplasia - more cells, driven by hormones or growth factors, or compensatory after damage or resection.
  • Metaplasia - one mature tissue replaced by another not native to the site, a reversible response to chronic irritation.
  • Atrophy - loss of cell size and number; causes include disuse, denervation, diminished blood supply, poor nutrition, loss of endocrine stimulation, pressure.

Weight training raises the workload on skeletal muscle, which cannot divide much, so it enlarges its existing fibres: hypertrophy. There are no new cells (not hyperplasia), no change of tissue type (not metaplasia), and the muscle is growing rather than shrinking (not atrophy).
b2-w5-ra-q7-7:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The four adaptations are told apart by what changes:

  • Hypertrophy - bigger cells, no new cells; the response of skeletal and cardiac muscle (limited division) to increased workload.
  • Hyperplasia - more cells, driven by hormones or growth factors, or compensatory after damage or resection.
  • Metaplasia - one mature tissue replaced by another not native to the site, a reversible response to chronic irritation.
  • Atrophy - loss of cell size and number; causes include disuse, denervation, diminished blood supply, poor nutrition, loss of endocrine stimulation, pressure.

Estrogen driving more endometrial glands is increased cell number in a hormone-sensitive organ under hormonal stimulation: hyperplasia. The glands multiply rather than simply enlarging, and they stay endometrium.
b2-w5-ra-q8-8:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The four adaptations are told apart by what changes:

  • Hypertrophy - bigger cells, no new cells; the response of skeletal and cardiac muscle (limited division) to increased workload.
  • Hyperplasia - more cells, driven by hormones or growth factors, or compensatory after damage or resection.
  • Metaplasia - one mature tissue replaced by another not native to the site, a reversible response to chronic irritation.
  • Atrophy - loss of cell size and number; causes include disuse, denervation, diminished blood supply, poor nutrition, loss of endocrine stimulation, pressure.

Chronic acid irritation replacing the esophagus's native squamous lining with intestinal-type epithelium is one mature tissue replaced by another not indigenous to that site: metaplasia. The change is in tissue type, not size or number.
b2-w5-ra-q9-9:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The four adaptations are told apart by what changes:

  • Hypertrophy - bigger cells, no new cells; the response of skeletal and cardiac muscle (limited division) to increased workload.
  • Hyperplasia - more cells, driven by hormones or growth factors, or compensatory after damage or resection.
  • Metaplasia - one mature tissue replaced by another not native to the site, a reversible response to chronic irritation.
  • Atrophy - loss of cell size and number; causes include disuse, denervation, diminished blood supply, poor nutrition, loss of endocrine stimulation, pressure.

Reduced brain volume from diminished blood supply is one of the lecture's named causes of pathologic atrophy: fewer and smaller cells, the opposite of both hyperplasia and hypertrophy.

b2-w5-sa-q6-6.html:
From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation. The baroreceptor reflex is a fast neural loop: stretch sensors send signals to the brain, which answers by changing heart rate or vessel diameter (TPR). High-pressure receptors sit in the aortic arch and carotid sinus and monitor blood pressure (B); low-pressure receptors sit in the atria and report blood volume to the same centre (C).

  • A - hormones are the slow arm of BP control; the reflex itself needs no adrenal hormone.
  • D - reversed: the aortic arch and carotid sinus are both high-pressure sites.
  • E - fails because A and D are false.

flags.title: Option C is garbled and only partly matches
flags.html: Option C lost its verb in transcription (“Signals from low pressure baroreceptors to the cardiovascular centre to monitor...”). 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation assigns the low-pressure (atrial) receptors to blood volume and the high-pressure ones to blood pressure, so C's “blood pressure and blood volume” overstates the note. The stem also reads as single-answer while the key has two.

b2-wb-fom-q77:
From 01 - An Introduction to Body Fluids Regulation. The lecture's dehydration logic runs in reverse here. Losing solute from the ECF makes the ECF hypo-osmotic, so water follows its gradient into the cells: ICF volume rises, ECF volume falls. Water keeps moving until the two compartments are iso-osmotic again, so osmolarity ends up lower in both - the cells cannot hold a different osmolarity from their surroundings.

  • A, D - ECF volume cannot rise when water is leaving it for the cells.
  • B - both volumes cannot fall with no net fluid loss; water shifts, it does not vanish.
  • C - right volumes, but osmolarity equilibrates, so it cannot fall in the ICF alone.
b2-wb-fom-q89:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. After injury, tissue either regenerates (normal function restored) or is repaired by scar. Regeneration happens in tissues made of labile and stable cells when the injury is not too severe - which covers most tissues (skin and GI epithelium constantly, hepatocytes from G0). Only permanent cells (cardiac myocytes, neurons, skeletal muscle) always heal by scarring.

  • A - fibrous scarring is the fallback for permanent cells, severe injury or damaged supporting structures, not the majority.
  • B, C - hyperplasia and hypertrophy are adaptations to stress (more cells, bigger cells), not the healing outcome after cell death.
b2-w6-meds2024-q13-13:
From 07 - Well Person Care and Screening for Cancer. The lecture defines screening in one sentence: we screen for relatively common problems in people who are asymptomatic, using cheap and easy tests, for conditions where early detection allows effective but less invasive treatment. A rare problem breaks that model - a test run on a low-prevalence population yields few true cases for the cost and many false positives.

  • A - cheap and easy: a stated feature.
  • B - asymptomatic population: a stated feature.
  • C - less invasive: stated, both of the test and of the treatment early detection allows.
b2-w6-meds2024-q16-16:
From 05 - Cancer From Macro to Molecular. The lecture lists the modifiable (“lifestyle”) risk factors: smoking, obesity, physical activity, diet, alcohol, injection drug use, sexual history (HPV and cervical cancer) and tanning beds (melanoma). Non-modifiable factors follow the GGRAPES mnemonic, whose R is reproductive history (breastfeeding, menarche, menopause), as spelled out in the chart in 03 - Cancer Genetics.

  • A - sexual activity: modifiable, via HPV exposure.
  • C - obesity: modifiable.
  • D - tanning beds: modifiable, melanoma.
  • E - smoking: the #1 modifiable risk factor.
b2-w6-new-q11-11:
From 04 - Diagnostic Pathway for Breast Mass (its benign-lesion table). The stem lists the terms as 1 Cyst, 2 Fibrocystic change, 3 Abscess, 4 Fibroadenoma.

  • A = 4, fibroadenoma - a benign neoplasm: a single nodule, well circumscribed and demarcated, firm and mobile.
  • B = 3, abscess - a collection of pus (acute inflammation, neutrophils) with warmth, redness, swelling and tenderness.
  • C = 1, cyst - a sac of air, fluid or semi-solid, well demarcated with smooth margins, collapsing when the fluid is drawn off.
  • D = 2, fibrocystic change - lumpy, nodular breasts whose pain or tenderness varies with the menstrual cycle; not a neoplasm.
b2-w6-new-q3-3:
From 04 - Diagnostic Pathway for Breast Mass. A cyst is a sac of air, fluid or semi-solid that is well demarcated and well circumscribed with smooth margins. Rough or irregular edges are the malignant feature in the lecture's benign-vs-malignant table, so B is false twice over: wrong margin, and the wrong inference from it.

  • A - true: the sac can hold air.
  • C - true: it collapses once the fluid is removed (e.g., by fine-needle aspiration).
  • D - true: well demarcated from surrounding tissue.
  • E - true: cysts can be single or multiple, as in fibrocystic change.
b2-w6-new-q8-8:
From 03 - Cancer Genetics. A tumour suppressor gene normally inhibits the cell cycle, slows proliferation or promotes apoptosis; cancer needs it lost (two hits, loss of function). Up-regulating the cycle describes an oncogene, so D is the false statement.

  • A - true: a proto-oncogene mutation is gain of function and one hit suffices.
  • B - true: tumour suppressor mutations are loss of function.
  • C - true: BRCA1 (chr 17) and BRCA2 (chr 13) are described as autosomal dominant.
  • E - true: promoting apoptosis is one of their normal roles.

b2-w6-sa-q11-11.html:
From 03 - Cancer Genetics. In p.L458X the “X” denotes a stop codon: leucine 458 is replaced by a premature stop, truncating the MSH2 protein. A point change that creates a stop is a nonsense mutation - the truncation the stem says causes colon cancer.

  • A - anticipation is earlier or worse disease each generation, a feature of triplet-repeat disorders (Block 1, 02 - Genetics); this is a point change, and the ages do not fall steadily.
  • C - affected relatives across generations on one side fit autosomal dominant hereditary cancer, which the lecture's red flags describe.
  • D - Audrey is the affected relative the lecture says to test first; once her mutation is known, relatives can be offered predictive testing.
  • E - X is a stop, not xanthine, which is not an amino acid.

flags.title: Nonsense-mutation notation is not in the notes
flags.html: 03 - Cancer Genetics covers hereditary red flags and testing an affected relative first, and Block 1's 02 - Genetics covers anticipation, but no note defines a nonsense mutation or the p.…X notation; that part is from general principles. The transcribed stem also lost the “>” in c.1373T>G, and option D names a sister although the stem gives Audrey only a brother.

b2-w6-sa-q4-4:
From 04 - Diagnostic Pathway for Breast Mass. A firm, mobile, non-tender 2.5 cm mass in a 28-year-old, stable for months and unchanged by feeding, is the lecture's fibroadenoma: a benign single nodule, well circumscribed, firm and mobile. Young age already makes a benign cause most likely.

  • A, J - abscess and mastitis are common in breastfeeding, but they are warm, red, swollen and tender.
  • E - a cyst is a smooth fluid sac, not described as a firm solid mass.
  • I - carcinoma is usually hard, irregular and may be fixed, and is less likely at 28.
  • G, L - a node would sit in the axilla; normal lactation change is diffuse, not a discrete lump.
  • B, C, D, F, K, M, N - remaining VITAMIN C&D categories with nothing in the history to support them.
b2-wb-fom-q132:
From 02 - Approach to Neoplasia. A neoplasm is an abnormal mass arising from excessive cell division and evasion of apoptosis. A slowly enlarging lump whose biopsy shows atypical cells with a raised mitotic rate is that - abnormal cells proliferating autonomously.

  • A - hypertrophy is larger cells with no new cells (05 - Cellular Stress & Repair).
  • B - hyperplasia is more cells, but normal ones driven by hormones or growth factors, not atypical ones.
  • C - metaplasia replaces one differentiated cell type with another; it adds no mass of atypical cells.
b2-w7-new-q16-16:
From 02 - Periodic Health Encounter for Older Adults. Hypercholesterolemia screening starts at 40 for men and 50 for women, repeated every 5 years if risk factors do not change other than age, with risk estimated by the Framingham calculator.

  • A - 40 is right for men only; women start later.
  • B - 50 is right for women only; men start earlier.
  • C - the ages are swapped between the sexes.
b2-w7-new-q18-18:
From 01 - Healthy Aging vs. Disease. The normal changes of aging include variable loss of cortical and spinal cord neurons with a decrease in brain weight and functional reserve, so an increase is not part of healthy aging.

  • A - normal: older adults shiver less, sense cold late, sweat less and vasoconstrict/vasodilate poorly.
  • B - normal: body water/fat ratio shifts, alongside reduced thirst and ADH sensitivity.
  • C - normal: pupils shrink and the lens thickens, lowering acuity and night vision.
  • E - normal: maximal heart rate falls with age, and the ventricles stiffen.

b2-w7-ra-q3-3.html:
From 07 - Introduction to Delirium. Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention with a precipitant to find, and the 4-AT scores an acute change or fluctuation on its own. Dementia is a decline that impairs independence in ADLs/IADLs and, by definition (03 - Mental Health Through Aging), does not occur exclusively during delirium - it develops over months to years, not hours to days.

  • A - IADL difficulty is the functional criterion for dementia, and an acutely delirious patient cannot manage IADLs either.
  • B, D, E - agitation, apathy and delusions can accompany either condition, so none separates them.

b2-w7-sa-q12-12:
From 09 - Interdisciplinary Teams & Community Resources for Older Adults. Home and Community Care (LHIN) care coordinators determine the right supports and coordinate long-term care admission (B), and it provides OHIP-funded nursing, OT, PT, social work and personal support at home - OTs assess function, mobility and safety in the home (C).

  • A - homemaking is a pay-per-service community service the LHIN coordinates access to, not one it provides at extra cost.
  • D - referral can come from the physician, patient or caregiver.
  • E - nothing in the lecture has home care giving daily medications; the lecture's answer to adherence is the pharmacist's blister packs.
  • F - false: home nursing is funded, which covers wound care.
b2-w7-sa-q17-17:
From 02 - Periodic Health Encounter for Older Adults, with the cervical program from Week 6's 07 - Well Person Care and Screening for Cancer. At 65 a woman is still inside the Pap program (25-70, every 3 years; A), is due lipids (women from 50, every 5 years; B), starts bone mineral density at 65 (C), and is screened for diabetes with HbA1c (E).

  • D, F - CBC and chest X-ray are on the lecture's explicit “not routinely ordered for screening” list, as is ECG.
  • G, K - magnesium and B12 are not screening tests in either lecture.
  • H, I, J - CT head, stress test and pelvic ultrasound are diagnostic tests with no screening role in a healthy woman.
b2-w7-sa-q3-3:
From 10 - Introduction to Neurofunction. First step: CNS or PNS. Leg hyperreflexia and upgoing plantars are upper motor neuron signs, so the lesion is central. Second step: the pattern. Weakness confined to both legs (paraparesis) localizes to the thoracic cord or lumbar roots; normal arm reflexes and power spare the cervical cord, and impaired leg vibration fits a cord lesion below the arms.

  • A - brainstem gives cranial nerve signs and usually affects the arms too.
  • B - a cervical lesion causes quadriparesis with arm UMN signs.
  • D - lumbar roots are LMN: reduced reflexes, no Babinski.
  • E - peripheral nerves are LMN too: hyporeflexia and atrophy, not hyperreflexia.
b2-w7-sa-q4-4:
From 10 - Introduction to Neurofunction. Impaired vision in the right hemifield of both eyes localizes behind the optic chiasm, since after the chiasm each optic tract carries the opposite hemifield from both eyes. The right hemifield travels on the left, ending in the left occipital lobe. She missed a car on her right for exactly this reason.

  • A, B - retina and optic nerve are anterior to the chiasm, giving loss in one eye only.
  • C - a chiasmal lesion hits the crossing fibres from both nasal retinas, taking out both temporal fields rather than one hemifield.
  • E - the right occipital lobe processes the left hemifield.

b2-w5-new-q16-16.html:
From 07 - Introduction to Laboratory Medicine. The lecture states that most laboratory errors occur in the pre-analytical phase - everything that happens before the analyser measures the sample: wrong sample type, wrong order of draw, under-filled tubes, tubes not mixed after collection, hemolysis, extreme temperature or improper storage, delayed transport, and long times from collection to analysis.

  • B - the analytical phase is the measurement itself; errors occur there but are the smaller share.
  • C - post-analytical errors (reporting, transcription, interpretation) are also real but not the largest source.
  • D - the lecture is explicit that the phases are not equal.

That is also why 10 - Approach to Abnormal Test Results checks pre-analytical explanations first when a value looks wrong.

b2-w5-new-q8-8.html:
From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation. The lecture splits blood pressure control in two: the autonomic nervous system is the short-term, rapid response, and hormonal mechanisms are the long-term, slow one. A fall in pressure unloads the high-pressure baroreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid sinus, and the brain responds by raising heart rate and sympathetic tone to the arterioles - raising CO and TPR, and so MAP (MAP = CO x TPR).

  • A, D - the RAAS and aldosterone are hormonal: renin must generate angiotensin II, and aldosterone works by changing Na+ reabsorption and volume - the slow arm.
  • B - a fall in GFR is a consequence of reduced renal perfusion, and any renal volume-conserving effect is slow, not a reflex.

b2-w5-sa-q1-1.html:
From 09 - Approach to Anxiety and Stress (charted as Effects of Stress and Inflammation on Blood Vessels). Sustained high pressure is hemodynamic stress on the endothelium; the vessel's repair response is intimal thickening, which narrows the lumen and cuts blood flow to the organ the vessel supplies. The complications are therefore vascular, organ by organ: atherosclerosis and MI, cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure, multi-infarct dementia, aortic dissection, cerebrovascular hemorrhage and renal failure.

  • B, C - renal failure and cerebrovascular disease are on the lecture's list.
  • A, E - erectile dysfunction and retinal hemorrhages are not named in the note, but they are the same small-vessel damage in the penile and retinal circulations.
  • D - cirrhosis is a disease of the liver parenchyma, not a consequence of arterial pressure.

b2-w5-sa-q2-2.html:
From 10 - Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees (Block 1). After migration a refugee must adjust to a new language and culture, secure housing and financial stability, and use a health system that is hard to access and poorly understood. Any of these can stop a blood test from happening, so an uncompleted requisition is a prompt to ask about barriers, not a sign of disinterest.

  • A, D - childcare and employment constraints (shift work, lost wages, no one to watch the children) compete with a lab visit during opening hours.
  • B - transit access decides whether she can physically reach the lab.
  • C - the lecture names not understanding the healthcare system and language barriers; a test whose purpose was never explained in her language is easy to set aside.
  • E - each is plausible, so all apply.

review.t: Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees

b2-wb-fom-q76.html:
From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation. The lecture's formula is MAP = DP + 1/3 (SP - DP). Here the pulse pressure is 160 - 93 = 67; a third of it is 22.3; and 93 + 22.3 = 115.3 mmHg.

  • A (114.7), B (121.4), D (109.3) - none follows from the formula.

The check worth remembering: MAP is weighted toward diastolic pressure, so it always sits below the simple average of systolic and diastolic (here 126.5). The abdominal pain in the stem is a distractor; the question is pure arithmetic.

b2-w6-meds2024-q14-14.html:
From 07 - Well Person Care and Screening for Cancer. For average-risk adults aged 50-74 (asymptomatic, no high-risk features), the screening test is the FIT - the fecal immunochemical test, which detects human heme (sensitivity 92.3%) - repeated every 2 years.

  • A - an incisional biopsy samples a known lesion; it is diagnostic, never a screen.
  • B - the lecture does list flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy every 10 years as an alternative, which is why this distractor is tempting, but it is not how the average-risk population is typically screened. High-risk patients (prior CRC or adenomatous polyps, IBD, a first-degree relative, FAP or Lynch) sit outside this program altogether.
  • D - false: CRC is on the screening schedule precisely because early detection changes outcomes.

review.t: Well Person Care and Screening for Cancer

b2-w6-new-q16-16.html:
From 06 - Communication of the Pathology Report. When a diagnosis is not clear-cut the pathologist writes a narrative report using a graded vocabulary of malignancy risk. The lecture's scale runs positive → suspicious → atypia (cannot exclude malignancy) → atypia (favour reactive) → negative; reversed for least-to-most:

  • 1 - E, negative for malignancy.
  • 2 - C, atypia present, favour reactive: abnormal cells, but the pathologist leans benign.
  • 3 - A, atypia present, cannot exclude malignancy: abnormal cells with malignancy left open.
  • 4 - B, suspicious for malignancy: probably cancer, short of certainty.
  • 5 - D, positive for malignancy.

The two atypia terms are the trap: favour reactive leans benign, cannot exclude does not.

b2-w6-new-q17-17.html:
From 03 - Cancer Genetics (its interprofessional management table). Numbering the answer list in the order shown, 1 = clinical geneticist through 11 = social worker:

  • A - 2, general surgeon: diagnostic biopsy, removal and staging, lymph node dissection.
  • B - 8, primary care physician: screening, symptom relief, counselling and referrals - the lecture's wording almost exactly.
  • C - 11, social worker: counselling through education, resources and supports, and advocacy in navigating recovery.
  • D - 6, palliative care physician: relieves suffering and improves quality of life in curable, chronic or life-threatening illness - at any stage, not only at the end of life.

The near-miss is C: the Indigenous health navigator (3) also counsels and advocates, but the lecture defines that role as navigating the health care system. The pathologist (7) makes the diagnosis on the tissue but does not perform the biopsy or the removal.

flags.title: The answer list lost its numbers
flags.html: The stem runs the eleven professions together without the numbers the key (A=2; B=8, C=11; D=6) refers to. The mapping above assumes they are numbered 1-11 in the order shown; check it against the original.

b2-w6-new-q7-7.html:
From 03 - Cancer Genetics (the surgical pathology report). The synoptic report is a concise, standardized checklist of the most important findings - the ones that predict outcome and guide treatment and further testing. The lecture lists its contents as specimen, tumour, margins, lymph nodes, stage, additional findings and comments.

  • A - specimen: the site and type of tissue.
  • B - tumour grade is recorded in the tumour section of the checklist.
  • C - margins show whether the excision was complete.
  • D - lymph node involvement feeds the stage.

All four are on the checklist, so E. 06 - Communication of the Pathology Report adds that synoptic reporting suits clear-cut diagnoses, while ambiguous ones get a narrative report.

b2-w6-new-q9-9.html:
Breast cancer 5-year survival falls with stage: essentially 100% at stage 1, about 92-93% at stage 2, about 72-74% at stage 3 and about 22-23% at stage 4 (Canadian Cancer Society figures). The shape follows the staging logic in 02 - Approach to Neoplasia: stage I has no nodal or distant spread, while stage IV means metastasis and is usually incurable.

  • A - false: 90% would put stage 1 below stage 2, which cannot be right.
  • B, C, D - match the published stage figures.
  • E - true; A and E cannot both hold, and E is the correct figure.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html:
No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

The stage-specific survival figures come from Canadian Cancer Society statistics, not a note.

b2-w7-meds2024-q15-15.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Basic ADLs are the self-care tasks, DEATH: Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting/continence, Hygiene. Instrumental ADLs are the more cognitively demanding tasks of running a household, SHAFT: Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/transportation.

  • C - housework is the H of SHAFT, an IADL.
  • A, B, D - toileting, dressing and eating are all DEATH items.

The distinction matters clinically: because IADLs need more cognitive skill, they are the first to need help as cognition declines (the Clinical Frailty Scale's “mildly frail” step is defined by it).

b2-w7-ra-q2-2.html:
From 07 - Introduction to Delirium (the embedded delirium note's risk factors). The material separates predisposing factors, which make a patient vulnerable, from precipitants (DIMESPPP), which tip them over. The predisposing list: cognitive impairment, comorbidity burden, age over 65, male sex, living in an institution, functional impairment, prior delirium, hearing and visual impairment, reduced education, alcohol use disorder, dehydration or malnutrition, and polypharmacy.

  • A - pre-existing dementia is cognitive impairment, the first item.
  • D - hearing impairment is on the list; it is also why glasses and hearing aids are part of management.
  • B, C, E - Crohn's disease, osteoarthritis and smoking are not named risk factors (arthritic pain would count as a precipitant, not a predisposition).

b2-w7-ra-q4-4.html:
From 07 - Introduction to Delirium. The lecture lists delirium's consequences as a longer length of stay; long-term cognitive and functional decline; higher mortality; and a higher risk of institutionalization, falls and ulcers, nursing time, and developing dementia.

  • B, E - both are on the list.
  • A - reversed: delirium increases nursing time per patient.
  • C - reversed: nothing lowers restraint use here; agitation and fall risk push it the other way.
  • D - stroke is a structural cause of delirium (the S of DIMESPPP), not a listed consequence.

b2-w7-sa-q13-13.html:
From 01 - Healthy Aging vs. Disease. Ageism is negative (or positive) stereotyping, prejudice or discrimination on the basis of age. The lecture's examples in care are clinicians under-treating illness as “normal aging” and patients under-reporting symptoms for the same reason. The keyed options are stereotypes of that kind:

  • A - “older adults overuse the system” frames their care as a burden.
  • C - “poor historians” leads clinicians to discount what the patient reports.
  • B - not a common ageist belief; if anything substance use is assumed to be a younger person's issue.
  • D - a statistic about living arrangements, not a belief.
  • E - as worded, the opposite of the ageist assumption, which is that illness is an expected part of aging.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html:
No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

01 - Healthy Aging vs. Disease defines ageism but does not list these five beliefs. If option E originally read “should expect to live with illness”, it would be an ageist belief and the key would be incomplete; check the source.

b2-w7-sa-q2-2.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Basic ADLs are DEATH - Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene - and the options use synonyms for some of them:

  • B Mobility and I Transfers - both are Ambulating, which the ADL note defines as moving from one position to another and walking independently.
  • E Grooming - Hygiene (bathing, grooming, dental, nail and hair care).
  • F Eating and J Toileting - named directly.
  • A, C, D, G, H - managing medications, shopping, cooking, housework and managing finances are IADLs (SHAFT plus medications), the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-w7-sa-q6-6.html:
From 08 - Frailty and Falls. The Clinical Frailty Scale turns on dependence. CFS 5, mildly frail, is more evident slowing with help needed for higher-order IADLs while basic ADLs remain independent. Mr Sandos's spouse has had to take over finances and medications because of his mistakes, he is independent in basic ADLs, and he walks with a cane after a fall. The lecture also notes that frailty corresponds to the degree of dementia, and his is mild.

  • A (3) - managing well means controlled medical problems and no dependence at all.
  • B (4) - vulnerable means not dependent on others for daily help; he now is, for IADLs.
  • D (6) - moderately frail needs help with all outside activities and housekeeping, stairs and bathing; his basic ADLs are intact.

Cooking and cleaning do not count against him: 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment says to judge change, and his spouse always did those.

b2-wb-fom-q94.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Ambulating is the A of DEATH, a basic ADL: moving from one position to another (transfers) and walking independently. It is physical self-care, not a household task that needs planning.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q95.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Cooking is the F of SHAFT (Food preparation), an IADL: it needs planning, sequencing and safety judgment, not just the physical ability to feed oneself. Do not confuse it with eating, which is a basic ADL.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q96.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Dressing is the D of DEATH, a basic ADL: selecting appropriate clothing and putting it on.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q97.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Eating is the E of DEATH, a basic ADL: the ability to feed oneself. Preparing the food is a different task - cooking is an IADL.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q98.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Finances are the A of SHAFT (Accounting), an IADL: the ability to pay bills and manage money, a cognitively demanding task of running a household rather than self-care.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q99.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Hygiene is the H of DEATH, a basic ADL: bathing and grooming oneself and keeping up dental, nail and hair care.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q100.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Managing medications is the extra M the SHAFT note adds to the IADLs: obtaining medications and taking them as prescribed. It depends on memory and organization rather than physical self-care.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q101.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Shopping is the S of SHAFT, an IADL: acquiring food and clothing.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q103.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Using the telephone is a T of SHAFT, an IADL, along with mail, internet and email.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q104.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Toileting is the T of DEATH, a basic ADL: getting to and from the toilet, using it appropriately and cleaning oneself, plus continence - control of bladder and bowel.
