The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q105.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Transportation is a T of SHAFT, an IADL: driving or using public transport.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q102.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Social engagement is not one of the named SHAFT items, but it belongs on the IADL side by the same logic: it is a higher-order activity of living in the community, not basic self-care of the body - and none of the DEATH items (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene) covers it.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html:
No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

The notes' ADL and IADL lists (DEATH, SHAFT plus medications) do not name social engagement; the IADL classification follows the key and the logic of the split, not a lecture statement.

b2-wb-fom-q131.html:
From 05 - Principles of Clinical Pharmacology (its prescription abbreviations table).

  • A PO - 5, orally.
  • B BID - 1, twice a day; the frequency series is q.d., b.i.d., t.i.d., q.i.d. for once to four times a day.
  • C PRN - 2, as needed; 01 - Approach To Prescribing adds that a PRN order still needs a maximum frequency.
  • D AC - 4, before meals; p.c. is after meals.
  • E OD - 3, right eye, paired with O.S. (left eye) and O.U. (both eyes).

OD is the trap: it reads like “once daily”, but the lecture's once-daily abbreviation is q.d.

flags.title: The meanings were fused onto option E
flags.html: The five meanings were run into option E during transcription, so E reads “OD 1) Twice a day 2) As needed ...”. The intended list is 1 Twice a day, 2 As needed, 3 Right eye, 4 Before meal, 5 Orally.

b3-w9-new-q19-19:
From 10 - Pharmacological Treatment of Anemias and 08 - Myelodysplastic Syndrome. Folate does all three jobs:

  • A DNA synthesis - as tetrahydrofolate it is the cofactor for uracil → thymine; deficiency hits rapidly dividing cells.
  • B RBC synthesis - that is why its lack produces megaloblastic anemia (large erythroid precursors with immature nuclei).
  • C methylation - methyl-THF donates its methyl group via methionine synthase (homocysteine → methionine), the pathway behind the body's methylation reactions, DNA included.

So D is the complete answer; E (A and B only) drops the methylation role.
b3-w9-new-q22-22:
From the sickle cell disease reference note (the lecture notes cover crises but not lifestyle advice). Vaso-occlusive episodes are triggered by dehydration, cooling of the skin, stress and infection, because cold slows flow and promotes sickling and vasoconstriction. The advice is therefore a warm compress, never a cold one, on an injury, and not swimming in cold water.

  • A - it is cold water, not warm, that patients should avoid.
  • B - a warm compress is the recommended physical measure.
  • D - wrong, because C is correct advice.

b3-w9-new-q7-7.html:
From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. Microcytosis means Hb synthesis has fallen behind cell division, from too little heme or too little globin. The differential is TAILS: thalassemia, anemia of chronic inflammation, iron deficiency, lead poisoning, sideroblastic anemia.

  • A iron deficiency, C sideroblastic, D lead - all reduce heme synthesis (lead acts through the sideroblastic mechanism), so F is right.
  • B hemolytic anemias - classed with the normocytic anemias (the D of ABCD in 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia) and are not a heme or globin synthesis defect, so they are not on TAILS.
  • E - fails because it includes B.

flags.title: Hemolysis is not always normocytic
flags.html: 06 - Approach to Hemolytic Anemia says hemolytic anemia can be microcytic, normocytic or macrocytic depending on the cause, and thalassemia itself involves hemolysis. The key holds for hemolysis as a category of causes, but B is not strictly impossible.

b3-w9-ra-q9-9:
From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. The discriminator is the normal RDW: thalassemia makes uniformly small cells, and its smear shows target cells and basophilic stippling, with normal platelets and an RBC count higher than in iron deficiency.

  • B iron deficiency - the Schulich pattern is high RDW (anisocytosis), low ferritin and often high platelets.
  • C hypothyroidism - an endocrine cause of macrocytosis (05 - Approach to Macrocytic Anemia).
  • D renal disease with impaired EPO (“APO” is a typo) - underproduction with no marrow pathology, a normocytic picture (04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia).

b3-w9-sa-q10-10.html:
From 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia and 08 - Myelodysplastic Syndrome. MDS is a marrow diagnosis: anemia without reticulocytosis leads to a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, and an abnormal marrow names MDS. The workup is CBC, ferritin, BM aspirate/biopsy, flow cytometry and cytogenetics, which feed the IPSS score that then decides treatment (supportive care for lower risk, hypomethylating agents or HSCT for higher).

  • A - chemotherapy before a tissue diagnosis and risk score skips both steps.
  • B, C - observation without a marrow sample cannot confirm MDS; an abdominal ultrasound adds nothing to the diagnosis in a symptomatic man with Hb 76.

b3-w9-sa-q6-6.html:
From 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis. A sleep study is the investigation for obstructive sleep apnea: the erythrocytosis history asks about snoring, gasping or stopped breathing at night, and the workup lists a sleep study to confirm OSA as a hypoxic, secondary cause.

  • A generalized anxiety disorder, B acute insomnia - clinical diagnoses from the history; polysomnography looks for a sleep-breathing or sleep-architecture disorder, not worry or short-term sleeplessness.
  • D hypothyroidism - a thyroid problem diagnosed with blood work, not a sleep study.

b3-w9-sa-q7-7:
From 05 - Approach to Macrocytic Anemia (prevention: folic acid in pregnancy) and the supplement table in 06 - Approach to Hemolytic Anemia (pregnancy dose 0.4 mg). Folate is the one nutrient given routinely to everyone pregnant or planning pregnancy, because demand rises and folate stores last only months.

  • B iron - requirements rise in pregnancy (3-4 mg/day), but iron is replaced when deficiency is found, not uniformly before conception.
  • C vitamin D, D essential fatty acids, E calcium - none is the universal preconception supplement the lectures name.
b3-wb-heme-q1:
From 01 - Hematopoiesis. Of the four, only erythroblasts are nucleated - they are the nucleated RBC precursors in the marrow, and they are absent from normal peripheral blood.

  • Reticulocytes - have extruded the nucleus; they keep only RNA and ribosomes (seen on supravital stain).
  • Erythrocytes - no nucleus, organelles or granules.
  • Thrombocytes - fragments of megakaryocytes; like RBCs they lack a nucleus, though they do have granules.

Every option that adds reticulocytes, erythrocytes or thrombocytes (A, B, D, E) is therefore wrong.
b3-wb-heme-q102:
From 08 - Radiation Oncology. The 4 Rs of radiobiology explain why fractionation works: repair of sublethal damage between fractions, repopulation between fractions, redistribution of cells into radiosensitive cell-cycle phases, and reoxygenation of hypoxic tumour cells. Repair and repopulation spare normal tissue; redistribution and reoxygenation sensitize the tumour.

  • A - the recycling slogan, not radiobiology.
  • C - swaps in “recalibration” for repopulation.
  • D - drops repopulation for “review”.
b3-wb-heme-q14:
From 10 - Pharmacological Treatment of Anemias. The liver holds 2-5 mg of B12 against a requirement of only 1-2 mcg per day, so stores last 3-5 years (08 - Myelodysplastic Syndrome agrees; 05 - Approach to Macrocytic Anemia rounds it to 3-4). That is why B12 deficiency after a diet change or gastrectomy appears years later.

  • A 1 month, B 6 months - closer to folate, whose 10-12 mg store lasts only 3-4 months.
  • C 1-2 years - too short for a store roughly a thousand times the daily need.

b3-wb-heme-q25.html:
From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. Alpha thalassemia is common in Southeast Asian and African populations; beta thalassemia in Mediterranean populations. Option C reads the blanks as “South-East Asia [and] Africa” and “Mediterranean”.

  • A - puts Africa nowhere and places Europe with alpha.
  • B - Australia is not an alpha-thal population, and beta is not SE Asian.
  • D - reverses the pair, putting Mediterranean on alpha.

flags.title: The two blanks were run together
flags.html: Each option's two answers lost their separator during transcription (e.g. “South-East Asia Africa, Mediterranean”), so where the first blank ends is inferred. The bank also stores no machine-readable key for this question; only the key line gives C.

b3-wb-heme-q9:
From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. Sideroblastic anemia is iron trapped in mitochondria around the precursor nucleus. Its acquired causes are toxins, vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency, MDS, chronic alcohol, drugs (anti-TB, alkylating chemotherapy) and lead poisoning - so B, C and D are all associated.

A hydroxyurea is not on that list. The lectures meet it as a treatment for sickle cell disease (04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia), where it raises HbF; it is also a drug cause of macrocytosis, not of ringed sideroblasts.
b3-wb-heme-q98:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. The lecture's features concerning for malignancy include every option: systemic symptoms such as weight loss over 10% (with fever, night sweats), generalized lymphadenopathy, an abnormal CXR (mediastinal mass, hilar adenopathy) and an abnormal CBC (lymphoblasts, cytopenias). Other red flags are fixed, non-tender, matted nodes of 2 cm or more, supraclavicular location, and nodes that do not settle after antibiotics.

So none of A-D can be the one that is not a red flag, which is what E's double negative says. Context matters: over 98% of enlarged nodes in primary care are benign, and these flags are what pick out the few needing biopsy.

b3-w10-ra-q6-6.html:
Blood products in Canada are collected, tested and supplied by two national operators: Canadian Blood Services for every province and territory except Quebec, and Héma-Québec within Quebec. 01 - Approach to a Bleeding Patient covers what happens next - the hospital blood bank tests and issues the right product to the right patient - but not who supplies it.

  • A Canadian Red Cross - ran the blood system until the tainted-blood inquiry led to its replacement in 1998.
  • C International Red Cross - does not run national blood supply.
  • D hospital blood banks - they store, crossmatch and issue units; they are not the supplier.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

b3-w10-sa-q8-8.html:
Partly from 01 - Approach to a Bleeding Patient, which makes the blood bank responsible for issuing the right product and the nursing staff for giving it to the right patient at the bedside. The acute hemolytic transfusion reaction note adds only that ABO incompatibility is often human error.

The single commonest error is at sample collection: the tube is drawn from one patient but labelled as another (wrong blood in tube). The lab then types and crossmatches correctly against the wrong person's blood, so every later check passes.

  • A laboratory testing errors, C supplier mislabelling - rare, because testing and unit labelling are controlled and double-checked.
  • D bedside misidentification - a real cause, but less frequent than a mislabelled sample.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

b3-w11-new-q1-1.html:
From 01 - Innate Immunity and WBCs. Macrophages live for months rather than hours, and the lecture credits them with extra killing tools that neutrophils lack: acidification of the phagosome by vacuolar ATPase, iron and manganese efflux, copper and zinc influx, and reactive nitrogen intermediates.

  • B fails: nitric oxide synthase making nitrogen radicals is listed under M1 macrophages, not neutrophils.
  • D fails: neutrophils are polymorphonuclear, with a multi-lobed nucleus.
  • A is also true: both are phagocytes, and the lecture contrasts them with NK cells, which “DO NOT phagocytose like neutrophils or macrophages”.

flags.title: Option A is also true
flags.html: 01 - Innate Immunity and WBCs supports A (both macrophages and neutrophils phagocytose) as well as the keyed C. The stem asks for similarities and differences but allows one answer, so the question has two defensible choices.

b3-w11-new-q11-11:
From 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis and 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. Low EPO puts this in the primary (marrow-autonomous) group, and acquired primary erythrocytosis is PV. V617F is found in only 90-95% of PV. JAK2 exon 12 mutations are the other qualifying lesion in major criterion 3, so a negative V617F does not exclude PV.

  • A overreaches for the same reason: exon 12 testing is still pending.
  • C fails: EPO receptor mutations (ECYT1) are a congenital primary cause, and congenital causes are very uncommon.
  • D fails: secondary erythrocytosis has normal or high EPO, not low.
b3-w11-new-q13-13:
From 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis. Secondary erythrocytosis needs something that drives EPO: hypoxia or an EPO-secreting lesion. A lipoma does neither. It is a benign fatty tumour with no EPO production.

  • A high altitude and B obstructive sleep apnea both cause systemic hypoxia, which drives renal EPO.
  • C pheochromocytoma is on the lecture's list of pathologic EPO producers, with RCC, HCC and cerebellar hemangioblastoma.

b3-w11-new-q2-2.html:
From 01 - Innate Immunity and WBCs. Neutrophils kill by iron restriction, by damaging the cell wall and membrane, and by oxidation with toxic free radicals. The keyed C casts the free radicals' role as disabling the bacterial respiratory and energy machinery.

  • A fails: NADPH oxidase does not act alone. Its superoxide becomes H2O2, which myeloperoxidase combines with a halide to make hypochlorite. The lecture calls it the NADPH oxidase/myeloperoxidase system.
  • D fails: an NADPH oxidase defect (chronic granulomatous disease) leaves phagocytosed bacteria undestroyed. The defect is in killing, not migration.
  • B is not addressed in the notes. See the flag.

flags.title: The key is not supported by the lecture, and B may also be true
flags.html: 01 - Innate Immunity and WBCs never says free radicals target bacterial cytochromes, so the keyed C is unverified. Option B looks transcription-damaged: “OH-” has probably lost its radical dot (OH·, the hydroxyl radical). As written, it is the textbook contrast between a highly reactive hydroxyl radical and a comparatively weak oxidant, H2O2, and so may also be true. Check the source before relying on the key.

b3-w11-new-q3-3.html:
From 01 - Innate Immunity and WBCs. PAMPs are recognized by the innate system through germline-encoded PRRs such as TLRs. Adaptive immunity recognizes antigens, the fine structural detail of molecules, through somatically recombined, clonal TCRs and BCRs. So C is false.

  • A: healthy cells express MHC I, which engages the NK inhibitory receptor, so the NK cell does not kill. That is the lecture's mechanism.
  • B: PRRs are found on the cell surface (TLR 2, 4, 5, 6) and on endosomes (TLR 3, 7, 8, 9).
  • D is true: TLR 3, 7, 8 and 9 recognize microbial and viral nucleic acids.

flags.title: Option B's wording does not match the lecture
flags.html: 01 - Innate Immunity and WBCs places PRRs on the cell surface and on endosomes (intracellular), not “extracellularly”. The word may be a transcription error for “intracellularly”. Soluble extracellular PRRs do exist, but the note does not cover them. Either way, C is the clearly false statement.

b3-w11-new-q4-4:
From 04 - Approach to Leukemia. All three are on the lecture's list of emergencies. The hematologist wants to hear about them the day an acute leukemia is found.

  • A DIC is especially tied to APL, whose promyelocyte granules release procoagulant and fibrinolytic activity. Early APL deaths are mostly from hemorrhage, often intracerebral.
  • B leukostasis: large, sticky blasts lodge in small vessels, causing dyspnea, hypoxia, confusion and visual change. It is managed with fluids, leukapheresis and cytoreduction.
  • C tumour lysis: high K, PO4 and urate with low Ca, leading to renal failure and arrhythmia. It is managed with hydration, rasburicase or allopurinol, and dialysis.

b3-w11-new-q6-6.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. Features that favour reactive neutrophilia: toxic granulation, toxic vacuolation and Döhle bodies, no promyelocytes or myeloblasts in the blood, and negative cytogenetic and molecular studies.

  • A a WBC above 30 favours neoplasia.
  • B raised eosinophils and/or basophils favour neoplasia, classically CML.
  • D Auer rods mark myeloid blasts, which means leukemia.

flags.title: Option A has lost its comparison sign
flags.html: Option A reads “WBC 30”. The source almost certainly read WBC >30 × 109/L, which is the neoplastic clue in 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. The answer is unaffected.

b3-w11-new-q9-9:
From 03 - Approach to Leukopenia. Febrile neutropenia is an oncologic emergency, and the most common serious complication in hematologic cancer and chemotherapy. You stabilize, draw blood and urine cultures, and start empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (imipenem or piperacillin-tazobactam) promptly, before the source is known.

  • A fails: viral reactivation (HSV, CMV, VZV) and fungal infection are listed complications, alongside bacterial infection.
  • C fails: constitutional neutropenia is benign and not associated with infection risk.
  • D therefore fails.
b3-w11-ra-q8-8:
From 04 - Approach to Leukemia and 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. An acute leukemia is a cancer of an early, blast-stage cell. In AML, myeloid cells fail to differentiate beyond the blast stage: the cell cycle arrests where cells normally proliferate, giving rapid proliferation and high turnover. The lineage runs myeloblast → promyelocyte → myelocyte → metamyelocyte → band → neutrophil.

  • B myelocytes and C metamyelocytes are later, more mature stages. Their excess in the blood is the left shift of CML or a reactive process, not an acute leukemia.
  • D bands and segmented granulocytes are mature cells.
b3-w11-sa-q1-1:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis and 04 - Approach to Leukemia. A middle-aged man with marked lymphocytosis (48 × 109/L), left upper quadrant pain (splenomegaly) and B symptoms has a mature lymphoproliferative disorder, most likely CLL, until proven otherwise. The diagnosis needs two things: mature lymphocytes on the peripheral blood film (smudge cells; immature cells would point to ALL), and clonality by peripheral blood flow cytometry.

  • B, E: liver or spleen biopsy is invasive and unnecessary when the clone is circulating.
  • D CT stages disease. It does not diagnose it.
  • F serum electrophoresis looks for a myeloma paraprotein.
  • G BCR-ABL is for CML, a myeloid disease.

b3-w11-sa-q3-3.html:
From 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis and 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. PV is diagnosed when all 3 major criteria are met, or the first 2 major plus the minor criterion. The major criteria are a raised Hb, a hypercellular marrow and a JAK2 mutation. The minor criterion is a subnormal EPO. Option A has a JAK2 mutation and a low EPO: the clonal driver and the primary-erythrocytosis pattern.

  • B: a high EPO points to secondary erythrocytosis, which argues against PV despite the JAK2 result.
  • C and D: without a JAK2 mutation, and with Hb 160 at the top of the female reference range, neither is diagnostic.

flags.title: Hemoglobin thresholds are borderline
flags.html: The PV criterion in 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis has lost its comparison sign (“Hb 165 (M)”), and the WHO threshold is usually given as greater than 165 g/L. Option A's Hb of exactly 165 therefore sits on the cut-off, and the erythrocytosis chart in 05 uses 170 g/L for men. A is still the only option combining JAK2 positivity with a low EPO. No option mentions the marrow criterion.

b3-w11-sa-q5-5:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. This is PV: Hb 190, all three lines raised, aquagenic pruritus, JAK2 positive, low EPO. Management is aimed at preventing thrombosis. Every patient gets ASA 81 mg daily and a hematocrit target under 0.45. At 51 with no prior thrombosis he is low risk, so the hematocrit is brought down by phlebotomy.

  • B hydroxyurea is cytoreduction for high-risk PV (age 60 or over, or prior thrombosis).
  • C IV chemotherapy is for acute leukemia and has no role in PV.

b3-w11-sa-q8-8.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. Fever, sore throat, cervical nodes, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes in a young adult is EBV mononucleosis until proven otherwise. The lecture's test for it is the Monospot. Flow cytometry on peripheral blood is the non-invasive way to settle reactive versus clonal lymphocytosis if the picture persists. It is kept for persistence after 4-6 weeks, so in practice the Monospot comes first.

  • A/B marrow biopsy and C/H node excision or FNA are invasive, which the stem excludes.
  • G EBV IgG marks past exposure, not acute infection.

flags.title: Options were duplicated in transcription
flags.html: A and B are identical (marrow biopsy), and so are E and F (peripheral blood flow cytometry). The keyed F is the same test as E. The IgG-versus-acute-serology point for G is not in the notes and comes from general principles.

b3-w12-meds2024-q2-2:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. Where a node sits tells you what it drains, and so what to look for. Inguinal nodes drain the lower abdomen, external genital skin, anal canal, lower third of the vagina and lower limb. The lecture's inguinal list leads with benign reactive nodes, STIs and skin or lower-limb infection. Inguinal nodes are also the only ones normally palpable in adults.

  • A tuberculosis is the classic cause of mediastinal nodes.
  • B breast carcinoma drains to the axillary nodes.
b3-w12-meds2024-q3-3:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. Axillary nodes drain the breast, upper limb and chest wall. The lecture lists breast cancer (adenocarcinoma) first among axillary causes, with melanoma and lymphoma. Axillary adenopathy should prompt a breast exam.

  • A tuberculosis sits with sarcoidosis under mediastinal nodes.
  • C STIs drain to the inguinal nodes. Syphilis appears under axillary and epitrochlear, but STIs as a group point to the groin.
b3-w12-meds2024-q4-4:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. The lecture's causes of mediastinal nodes are Mycobacterium tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and primary or secondary malignancy. Hilar or mediastinal adenopathy on CXR is also one of the features concerning for malignancy.

  • B breast carcinoma spreads first to the axillary nodes.
  • C STIs drain to the inguinal nodes.
b3-w12-new-q16-16:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. The mediastinum is the space between the lungs, bounded by the thoracic inlet above and the diaphragm below. The anterior compartment, between sternum and pericardium, contains the thymus, internal thoracic arteries, lymph nodes, connective tissue and fat (“I CAN'T”). The tongue is in the oral cavity, above the thoracic inlet, so it is not in the mediastinum at all.

  • A, C, D, E are all listed anterior-mediastinal contents.
b3-w12-new-q17-17:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. For suspected ectopic thyroid tissue or goitre, the lecture says to consider a technetium scan, which shows functioning thyroid tissue. MRI's role is to distinguish compression from invasion of structures.

  • A is true: CT chest with IV contrast is the standard next step after a plain-film abnormality.
  • B is true: PET/CT if lymphoma is suspected.
  • C is true: scrotal ultrasound if a germ cell tumour is suspected.
  • E is true: a widened mediastinum is 6 cm or more on an upright PA film (8 cm on a supine AP film).
b3-w12-new-q19-19:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies. Antimetabolites (methotrexate, 5-FU, 6-MP, 6-thioguanine) interfere with nucleic acid metabolism, so the nucleotides needed to build DNA and RNA are not made. 5-FU's block of thymidine synthesis is the classic example.

  • A garbles the mechanism: alkylators cross-link guanine so strands cannot separate. They do not convert hydrogen bonds.
  • C preventing DNA relaxation is topoisomerase inhibition (anthracyclines, etoposide), not alkylation.
  • D intercalation belongs to the antitumour antibiotics. Topoisomerase inhibitors act by blocking topoisomerase.
  • E taxanes stabilize microtubules to cause M-phase/metaphase arrest, not prophase.
b3-w12-new-q20-20:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies. Nivolumab is a PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor. The lecture lists checkpoint inhibitors for myeloma, Hodgkin lymphoma and lung cancer, not T-cell lymphoma, so E is the mismatched pair.

  • A daratumumab (anti-CD38) targets plasma cells in myeloma.
  • B, C rituximab (anti-CD20) treats CLL and follicular lymphoma, like any B-cell malignancy.
  • D Zevalin, the radio-conjugated anti-CD20 mAb, is used for relapsed follicular lymphoma.
b3-w12-new-q5-5:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. Most enlarged nodes are reactive: over 98% in primary care are non-malignant. So the first step is history and physical, not a test. Location tells you the drainage area to examine. A neck node leads to the oral cavity, oropharynx and scalp. The history screens for constitutional symptoms and exposures, and the exam checks size and character: hard or soft, tender, mobile or fixed.

  • A, B CT and X-ray come after the clinical assessment, guided by what it finds.
  • D biopsy is for nodes with red flags, and FNA is not the lecture's preferred biopsy anyway.
b3-w12-new-q7-7:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. Several features on the lecture's list are concerning for malignancy:

  • A systemic symptoms: fever over a week, night sweats, weight loss over 10%.
  • C fixed, non-tender, matted nodes.
  • E a supraclavicular node, which drains the GI tract, GU tract and lungs, so think abdominal or thoracic malignancy.
  • B is not a red flag. Regional (localized) nodes usually reflect infection in the drainage area. It is generalized lymphadenopathy that is concerning.
  • D is not either. Tenderness suggests an inflammatory or reactive node, and the worrying node is non-tender.
b3-w12-new-q9-9:
From 04 - Classification and Testing for Lymphomas. Reed-Sternberg cells are scattered in a mostly reactive background and do not express light-chain monoclonality. Flow cytometry therefore sees only polyclonal lymphocytes, reads as normal, and cannot detect classical HL.

  • A immunohistochemistry is how classical HL is shown: CD15+ and CD30+, with CD20 and CD45 negative.
  • C FISH is one of the three standard ancillary tests (with IHC and flow) used for diagnosis and prognosis in lymphoma.
b3-w12-sa-q1-1:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies.

  • i Imatinib: D (CML). This tyrosine kinase inhibitor blocks the constitutively active BCR-ABL made by t(9;22).
  • ii ATRA: A (APL). APL's PML-RARA fusion arrests maturation at the promyelocyte stage, and ATRA dissociates that block so the cells differentiate.
  • iii Nivolumab: C (Hodgkin lymphoma). This PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor is listed for HL, myeloma and lung cancer.
  • iv Ibrutinib: B (CLL). This Bruton kinase inhibitor is used for CLL specifically.

b3-w12-sa-q6-6.html:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies.

  • i Imatinib: B (diarrhea), with muscle cramps, periorbital edema, cytopenias and effusions.
  • ii Rituximab: D (infusion reactions), the remaining pair once the others are placed.
  • iii ATRA: A (differentiation syndrome). ATRA drives all the leukemic promyelocytes to mature at once, which is why the lecture says it is given with chemotherapy to prevent a very high WBC count.
  • iv Nivolumab: C (colitis). PD-1 blockade releases immune toxicity: colitis, pneumonitis, rash, hepatitis, hypophysitis, nephritis. It is treated with steroids.
  • v Ibrutinib: E (bruising), with atrial fibrillation. Ibrutinib also causes diarrhea, so bruising is the discriminating match.

flags.title: Two pairings are only partly in the notes
flags.html: The note does not mention rituximab infusion reactions or name “differentiation syndrome”. It only describes the mass differentiation that ATRA causes. These two pairs are reasoned by elimination and general principles.

b3-w12-sa-q9-9.html:
From 07 - Individual Variability in Drug Response (Week 8). A clinically actionable pharmacogenetic pair is one where the genotype changes the dose or the drug choice. Ethanol metabolism through ADH is not used this way, so D is the odd one out.

  • A CYP2C9 metabolizes the active S-warfarin. Its variants (*2, *3) cut clearance by up to 85% and are present in up to 18% of people. Together with VKORC1, it underlies genotype-guided warfarin dosing, which LHSC offers.
  • B clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19 (PoM 1 08 - PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs), so poor metabolizers get less antiplatelet effect.
  • C DPYD deficiency blocks 5-FU breakdown, causing severe toxicity.

flags.title: Partly not covered by the notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers DPYD and 5-fluorouracil, or ADH and ethanol, so those lines come from general principles. Verify them before relying on them.

b3-wb-heme-q96:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. The 5 T's of an anterior mediastinal mass are thymus/thymoma, “terrible” lymphoma, teratoma/germ cell tumour, thyroid and thoracic aortic aneurysm. A tracheal growth is not one of them, and the trachea is not an anterior-compartment structure.

  • A thymus: thymomas are about 20% of mediastinal masses, slow-growing, and linked to myasthenia gravis.
  • B lymphoma, Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin.
  • D thyroid: goitre, thyroiditis or neoplasm.
  • E thoracic aorta: an aneurysm can present as an anterior mass.

b3-wb-heme-q99.html:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. The workbook's options read Size < 3 cm and Persistence > 4 weeks; the portal copy lost both signs. With them restored, A is the only feature that is not a red flag: a smaller node is reassuring, and the lecture's size threshold for concern is a non-tender node ≥ 2 cm that is growing or not settling after 2 weeks of antibiotics.

  • B persistence: a node that fails to resolve is concerning.
  • C supraclavicular nodes drain the chest and abdomen, so think thoracic or abdominal malignancy.
  • D, E hard, fixed (immobile), matted, non-tender nodes are the malignant character on exam.

flags.title: Option text lost its signs
flags.html: The workbook note reads A) Size < 3 cm and B) Persistence > 4 weeks, and its key line says “concerning if size was >3cm”. As printed here, a 3 cm node would itself be a red flag (the lecture's threshold is ≥ 2 cm). The key is right for the original wording.

b3-w9-new-q21-21:
From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. In beta thalassemia the unpaired excess alpha chains precipitate in red-cell precursors and circulating cells. The lecture lists all three consequences under thalassemia: ineffective erythropoiesis, hemolysis, and iron overload, so D is correct.

  • A ineffective erythropoiesis: precursors die in the marrow, and the marrow expands in response (bone deformities, short stature).
  • C hemolysis: damaged cells are cleared early, giving jaundice and splenomegaly.
  • B iron overload: from transfusion and increased absorption driven by the ineffective erythropoiesis, hence chelation with deferoxamine.

b3-w9-sa-q8-8.html:
From 01 - Hematopoiesis (abnormal RBC morphology). The image is not reproduced here, but per the key it shows sickle cells: elongated cells with pointed ends and no central pallor. They form because the HbS beta-globin mutation (position 6 Glu to Val) lets deoxygenated hemoglobin polymerize and stretch the cell. An 8-year-old fits too, since HbF protects until about age 3.

  • B thalassemia major gives a hypochromic microcytic film with target cells, teardrops and basophilic stippling, not sickled forms.
  • C thalassemia minor is mild and hypochromic, with a normal RDW and a high RBC count.
  • D HbC (Glu to Lys) is named in the lecture, but no film feature is given for it; sickled cells point to HbS.

flags.title: Image not available
flags.html: The question refers to a blood film that is not shown in the bank; the explanation relies on the key's statement that it shows sickled red cells.

b3-wb-heme-q26.html:
From 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia. The key gives A, C, D, F. Sickle cell disease is a chronic hemolytic anemia (A). Sickled, adhesive cells cause sickle and vaso-occlusive crises (C, D: dactylitis, acute chest syndrome, stroke). Chronic organ damage explains the shorter life expectancy (F).

  • I is backwards: heterozygotes have increased resistance to malaria.
  • E, H IBS and COPD are unrelated to sickling.
  • G bronze skin belongs to iron-overload states (hemochromatosis), not sickle disease; jaundice is the hemolytic skin sign.
  • B fever is not listed in the lecture as a sickle feature. It signals a complication (infection, acute chest), and it is the likeliest intended fifth answer.

flags.title: Stem asks for five; the key gives four
flags.html: The question says “Choose 5” but the workbook key lists only A, C, D and F, and the bank records no correct letters for grading. Fever (B) is the most plausible fifth, but no lecture note says so.

b3-w10-ra-q8-8:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia and 02 - Hemostasis. Warfarin blocks VKORC1, so factors II, VII, IX and X are not activated. FVII has the shortest half-life, so the extrinsic pathway falls first, and the PT rises. The INR standardizes the PT across labs specifically to monitor vitamin K antagonists (target 2.0-3.0).

  • A the aPTT monitors UFH and the IV direct thrombin inhibitors.
  • C fibrinogen is not a vitamin K-dependent factor.
  • D D-dimer measures fibrin breakdown; a negative result is used to exclude VTE, not to dose drugs.
b3-w10-sa-q10-10:
From 01 - Hematopoiesis (components of blood). Plasma is the non-cellular fluid of blood: water, albumin, coagulation factors and immunoglobulins. Serum is what is left after the blood has clotted, which is plasma minus the coagulation factors and fibrinogen used up in the clot. That is also why coagulation tests are drawn into a citrate (blue-top) tube and run on plasma.

  • B complement proteins are present in both.
  • C, D both plasma and serum are cell-free. Erythrocytes and platelets are spun out of plasma, and they are trapped in the clot for serum.
b3-w10-sa-q6-6:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia. LMWH is the lecture's indication for long-term treatment of cancer-associated thrombosis, and cancer-associated VTE is treated for a minimum of 6 months, stopping only if the cancer is cured.

  • A the lecture names warfarin for renal failure. In active cancer, interactions and variable nutrition make INR control unreliable.
  • C UFH is an IV, hospital drug with aPTT monitoring 2-4 times a day, so it is not a long-term option.
  • D aspirin is an antiplatelet drug (it blocks COX and lowers thromboxane A2), and it is not a treatment for venous thrombosis.
b3-wb-heme-q107:
From 01 - Approach to a Bleeding Patient (blood components). The lecture's platelet contraindications are refusal; not indicated; and TTP, HUS, HIT, so all four options apply.

  • A transfusion requires written informed consent from a capable patient, so refusal ends it.
  • B a normal count without bleeding is not an indication. Platelets are given at < 10, for symptomatic or massive bleeding, or before surgery at < 50 (neurosurgery < 100).
  • C, D TTP and HUS are consumptive, clotting microangiopathies, and transfused platelets feed further thrombosis. The same applies to HIT.

b3-w11-new-q10-10.html:
From 03 - Approach to Leukopenia. The lecture numbers the febrile neutropenia protocol in this order:

  • 1. C stabilize - ABCs, IV fluids, and O2 for hypoxia.
  • 2. B investigate - CBC and differential, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, transaminases and bilirubin, blood and urine cultures, and a CXR.
  • 3. A focused history and exam - mouth, pharynx and sinuses, lungs, GI (no DRE), GU, skin and catheter sites, and mental status.
  • 4. D empiric antibiotics - IV imipenem or piperacillin-tazobactam, adding vancomycin for a line or skin infection or instability.

Cultures come before antibiotics so the organism can still be grown, but the antibiotics must not be delayed: this is an oncologic emergency.

b3-w11-new-q12-12.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. Every PV patient gets ASA 81 mg daily and a target Hct below 0.45, and the risk category then decides everything else. High risk (age ≥ 60 or prior thrombosis) means hydroxyurea with or without phlebotomy. Low risk means phlebotomy. At 45 with no prior clot she is low risk, so she needs phlebotomy plus ASA.

  • A - leaves out the ASA that every patient receives.
  • C, D - hydroxyurea (cytoreduction) is reserved for high-risk patients, and she is not one.

b3-w11-new-q15-15.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis and 10 - In-Class. The lecture gives primary myelofibrosis a characteristic blood film: teardrop cells (A) and a leukoerythroblastic picture (B), usually with splenomegaly and cytopenias.

  • C reticulin fibres - these are a marrow finding. Reticulin or collagen fibrosis (grade 2/3) on the core biopsy is a major diagnostic criterion, but fibres do not circulate and cannot be seen on a blood film.
  • D - pairs a true film finding with that marrow finding.

As the stem is worded, the supportable set is A and B, and no option offers that pair.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key is E, which includes C. 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis places reticulin fibrosis on the marrow biopsy (a PMF major criterion), not on the blood film, which shows teardrops and a leukoerythroblastic picture. The key only works if the stem means “film or marrow”. As written, A and B are the true findings, and no option offers that pair.

b3-w11-new-q16-16.html:
From 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia.

  • A true - dyskeratosis congenita is one of the two hereditary forms the lecture names, with Fanconi anemia. It presents with oral leukoplakia, nail dystrophy and lacy pigmentation.
  • B false - aplastic anemia is marrow failure: a hypocellular marrow replaced by fat, most often idiopathic. It is not a clonal neoplasm, which is what separates it from MDS (an abnormal marrow) and from myelophthisis (a replaced marrow).
  • C true as keyed - aplastic anemia is more common outside Western countries.

With A and C true and B false, the answer is D, and E fails because of B.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: No lecture note gives regional incidence figures for aplastic anemia, so statement C (Mexico vs the United States) rests on general knowledge. Verify it before relying on it.

b3-w11-new-q8-8.html:
From 04 - Approach to Leukemia. In tumour lysis, dying tumour cells spill their contents into the blood. High K causes arrhythmia. High PO4 binds calcium, and the resulting hypocalcemia causes seizures and arrhythmia. Uric acid and phosphate injure the kidney, and the result is metabolic acidosis, renal failure and death, which together amount to multiorgan failure.

  • A decreased tissue perfusion - the mechanism of leukostasis: large, sticky blasts lodge in small vessels and cause local hypoxemia.
  • B very high blast count - a risk factor for TLS and leukostasis, not a consequence of either.
  • D intracranial hemorrhage - the typical early death in APL, caused by DIC.

b3-w11-ra-q4-4.html:
From 06 - Multiple Myeloma. The spine is the most common site of myeloma bone disease, so back pain with tender vertebrae fits. Add anemia below 100 g/L (the A of CRAB) and rouleaux on the film, and the picture is myeloma. The next steps are SPEP/UPEP for an M spike, serum free light chains, calcium and creatinine, and a skeletal survey.

  • B follicular lymphoma - indolent painless lymphadenopathy. It causes neither rouleaux nor vertebral disease.
  • C AML - marrow failure with circulating blasts. It can cause sternal bone pain, but rouleaux are not an AML finding.
  • D MDS - cytopenias with dysplasia in an older patient, and no paraprotein to stack the red cells.

b3-w11-sa-q2-2.html:
From 04 - Approach to Leukemia and 10 - In-Class. Auer rods are the finding that marks a blast as myeloid. The AML film shows large blasts with Auer rods, and they are how the lecture tells M blasts from L blasts, with flow cytometry to confirm. The CBC here already shows blasts, so seeing Auer rods is what makes it AML.

  • B BCR-ABL - t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome of CML.
  • C JAK2 - the driver of the MPNs (PV in 90-95% of cases, ET and PMF in 50-60%).
  • D dysplasia - the defining feature of MDS, not of AML.

b3-w11-sa-q4-4.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. A raised WBC count does not say which white cell is raised. The lecture says that is exactly what the differential is for, and its approach begins by sorting the cells by lineage (neutrophil, lymphocyte, eosinophil and so on) and by maturity. Every later decision depends on that answer.

  • A reticulocyte count - measures red cell production and is used to work up an anemia. Her hemoglobin is normal.
  • B INR - a coagulation test with no bearing on the white count.
  • D flow cytometry - establishes clonality later, for example in a lymphocytosis that persists after 4-6 weeks or when blasts are seen. It is not a first test.

b3-w11-sa-q6-6.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. Granulocytes mature through myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band and neutrophil, and all of those stages belong in the marrow. The lecture says only fully developed neutrophils should be seen in the peripheral blood.

Having no myeloblasts or promyelocytes in the blood is one of the features of a reactive process. Any circulating blasts favour a neoplasm, which is why 10%, 5% and 3% are all abnormal. Even the “under 10%” blast count of chronic-phase CML is a disease finding, not a normal range.

b3-w11-sa-q7-7.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis and 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis. Itching after a bath or shower is aquagenic pruritus, and early satiety with abdominal discomfort suggests splenomegaly. In a man over 60 with fatigue, that is the lecture's picture of polycythemia vera, and JAK2 (V617F or exon 12) is present in 90-95% of cases.

  • A Philadelphia chromosome - CML, which presents with a high WBC and basophilia rather than aquagenic itch.
  • B t(15;17) - APL, an acute leukemia that presents with bleeding and DIC.
  • C marrow fibrosis - PMF also causes early satiety and splenomegaly, but it is not linked to aquagenic pruritus and carries JAK2 in only 50-60% of cases. JAK2 is the more likely finding.

b3-w12-new-q10-10.html:
From 04 - Classification and Testing for Lymphomas (the table of main differences between HL and NHL).

  • i true - classical HL spreads contiguously, from one node to the adjacent node. NHL can spread contiguously or non-contiguously.
  • ii false - the statement is reversed. HL is nodal, and extranodal disease is rare. NHL is the one that is nodal or extranodal.
  • iii true - in classical HL all cells are mature, while NHL can be mature (lymphocytic) or immature (lymphoblastic).

So the true statements are i and iii, which is B.

flags.title: Statements ii and iii have lost their numerals
flags.html: Only the first statement carries its label (“i)”). The other two appear as a numbered list (1, 2) below it, so read list item 1 as ii and item 2 as iii when matching them to the options.

b3-w12-new-q15-15.html:
From 06 - Multiple Myeloma. R-ISS stage 3 requires β2-microglobulin ≥ 5.5 together with high-risk FISH or a high LDH. The high-risk FISH abnormalities the lecture lists are t(4;14), t(14;16) and del(17p).

  • A t(4;14) and C t(14;16) - both on that high-risk list, so both point towards stage 3.
  • B t(14;6) (usually written t(6;14)) and D t(11;14) - neither is on the list, so neither makes a patient stage 3. These are the abnormalities that do not indicate R-ISS 3.

flags.title: The key gives two letters, but option E already combines them
flags.html: The bank keys this as “B, D”, yet option E is “B and D”. Read as a single-best-answer question, the intended choice is E. The two agree in content.

b3-w12-new-q21-21.html:
From 08 - Radiation Oncology and 04 - Classification and Testing for Lymphomas. Early-stage HL is now treated with combined-modality therapy: a short course of chemotherapy followed by involved-field radiation. Radiation doses and field sizes are being reduced, especially in favourable cases, and bulky disease is treated like advanced disease.

  • A - radiation alone (sub-total nodal irradiation) was the historical cure. It was abandoned because of late toxicity: second cancers and cardiac disease.
  • B - gets the order backwards. Chemotherapy comes first.
  • C and D - both describe chemotherapy before radiation, the lecture's sequence. The notes do not give cycle numbers.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key is D, but the bank's own note says “chemotherapy for unfavourable is 4 cycles”, which makes D (“2 cycles”) false as written. 08 - Radiation Oncology supports chemotherapy before radiation for favourable early-stage disease, which is what C says. The notes give no cycle counts. In the standard regimen (from general knowledge, not the notes), favourable disease gets 2 cycles and then radiation, and unfavourable disease gets 4. On that reading C is the answer. Check the lecture slides.

b4-w13-new-q7-7.html:
From 01 - Homeostatic Control of Body Temperature. The note frames thermoregulation as a negative-feedback loop: thermoreceptors → hypothalamus → effectors, holding the regulated variable at its set point.

  • Effector → D: sweat glands carry out heat loss.
  • Thermoreceptors → B: sensory neurons activated by warmth or cold, found in the skin, spinal cord, abdominal viscera and brain.
  • Regulated variable → A: core temperature held at about 37°C (normal 35.5-37.7°C).
  • Feedforward → C: this pairing is left by elimination. The note defines feedforward as the body acting in anticipation of a thermal change (e.g. responding to a cold breeze before core temperature drops).

flags.title: Option C is a poor fit for feedforward
flags.html: 01 - Homeostatic Control of Body Temperature defines a feedforward mechanism as acting before the change happens. “Body temperature during hyperthermia” is a state of the regulated variable, not an anticipatory response, so the fourth pairing only works by elimination. Learn the definition, not this pairing.

b4-w13-sa-q2-2.html:
From 03 - Innate Immunity Refresher. Antigen from an organism a macrophage has ingested is handled by the antigen-presenting-cell route. The APC internalises the organism, breaks it into peptides with lysosomal enzymes, and displays them in the groove of MHC class II (HLA class II) to CD4+ helper T cells. The note restricts MHC II to APCs such as macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells.

  • B: MHC class I samples the cell's own internal contents for CD8+ T cells, not phagocytosed material.
  • C, D, E: cytosolic proteases, the endoplasmic reticulum and TAP transporters are the loading machinery of that class I route, so they go with B.

flags.title: The class I machinery is not in the notes
flags.html: 03 - Innate Immunity Refresher supports A (lysosomal processing onto MHC II in APCs). It does not describe the proteasome, TAP or ER loading steps of class I presentation, so the reasoning against C-E comes from general immunology.

b4-w13-sa-q5-5.html:
From 03 - Innate Immunity Refresher. Co-stimulation is the APC's second signal, B7 (CD80/86) binding CD28, delivered alongside TcR-antigen-MHC binding. It drives the helper T cell into growth and clonal proliferation, largely through more IL-2 and IL-2 receptors. Part of what keeps the activated clone expanding is pro-survival proteins such as Bcl-XL.

  • A: loading antigen into MHC II is the first signal's job, done by the APC before co-stimulation matters.
  • B: anergy is what happens when co-stimulation is blocked (09 - Autoimmunity, 06 - Approach to Allergy: CD28:CD80 blockade).
  • D: co-stimulation increases IL-2 transcription rather than inhibiting it.
  • E: activated T cells ramp up metabolism for proliferation. They do not slow it.

flags.title: Bcl-XL is not in the notes
flags.html: The notes cover co-stimulation through B7-CD28 and IL-2, and anergy when it is blocked, which rules out B and D. The Bcl-XL survival mechanism in the keyed option is not mentioned in any Block 4 note, so that part is from general immunology. Verify it before relying on it.

b4-w13-sa-q6-6:
From 10 - Approach to the Assessment of a Patient with Fever. The rule is to investigate when the diagnosis is uncertain. Dysuria, frequency and urgency with no fever or flank pain look like simple cystitis, but a new sexual partner puts urethritis from N. gonorrhoeae or C. trachomatis on the differential, and those present the same way. So test the site of inflammation:

  • Urinalysis/dipstick: the targeted test the lecture names for suspected UTI.
  • Urine culture and sensitivity: confirms the organism and guides the antibiotic.
  • NAAT for GC/CT: the molecular test for an STI, which culture of urine will not find.

E fails for this patient: the lecture allows skipping culture only for a clearly likely UTI, and the sexual history makes this one unclear.
b4-w13-sa-q8-8:
From 02 - Classification of Different Microbes. The note gives one seven-step cycle for virtually all viruses: attachment → entry → uncoating → protein synthesis → genome replication → assembly → release.

The logic fixes the order. The genome must be uncoated before the host ribosomes can translate it. Viral proteins, including the polymerases, are needed to replicate the genome. Only then can new genomes and structural proteins be assembled into virions.

  • A, B, C put protein synthesis before uncoating, which cannot happen while the genome is still inside the capsid. C also assembles virions before there are genomes to package.
  • E replicates the genome before making the proteins that replication depends on.
reviews-b4-Q12:
From 14 - Pathology of Acute Inflammation. An abscess is walled off, and its pus-filled necrotic centre has no blood vessels, so antibiotics struggle to reach it. That is why the definitive treatment is incision and drainage: open the skin and clear the contents. Deep organ abscesses may need a more invasive surgical approach.

In-Class - Fever gives the S. aureus-specific reason. Coagulase and fibrinogen-binding proteins build a fibrin pseudocapsule around the abscess community, which keeps leukocytes out and blocks antibiotics. Abscesses therefore will not resolve on antibiotics alone. Antibiotics follow drainage, to treat surrounding cellulitis or spread, and contact precautions apply if the patient is flagged for MRSA.
b4-w14-meds2024-q11-11:
From 01 - Transmission of Infectious Agents and 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. Herd immunity protects the few susceptible people because the pathogen is unlikely to find them. The proportion who must be immune depends on the agent's transmissibility. Highly infectious, high-R0 diseases such as measles need the highest coverage. Measles is airborne, and transmission has been reported up to 90 minutes after the index case left the room.

  • B: a short incubation period changes how fast an outbreak unfolds, not how many secondary cases each case produces.
  • C: lethality is not transmissibility. A virus that kills its host is not thereby easier to spread.
  • D: a stable antigen, if anything, makes durable herd immunity easier to reach, not harder.
b4-w14-meds2024-q12-12:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. Sepsis is organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response. The cardiovascular picture is tachycardia with hypotension, as the heart compensates for arteriolar vasodilation and capillary leak, so a falling heart rate is the odd one out.

  • A: low BP from vasodilation and loss of intravascular fluid. When it does not respond to fluids, it is septic shock.
  • C: oliguria is the kidney pillar of early recognition.
  • D: hypoxia (and ARDS) is the lung pillar, alongside tachypnea.
  • E: microcirculatory dysfunction clogs capillaries, so tissues are underperfused, the mechanism behind multi-organ failure.

b4-w14-meds2024-q14-14.html:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. The lecture separates early treatment (early, appropriate, broad-spectrum antibiotics) from life support, which is invasive support for failing organs that buys time and fixes nothing. Vancomycin is an antibiotic that treats the infection itself, so it belongs to early treatment, not life support.

  • Vasopressors: cardiovascular support for hypotension that fluids have not corrected.
  • Dialysis (or CRRT): renal support.
  • Mechanical ventilation: pulmonary support, along with prone positioning, lung-protective ventilation and ECMO.

flags.title: The bank's key line misnames vancomycin
flags.html: The key line calls vancomycin an “antibody treatment”. It is an antibiotic (a glycopeptide that blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking; 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1). The keyed letter is right, but the reason given with it is not.

b4-w14-meds2024-q16-16:
From 02 and 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely. MRSA carries mecA, which makes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein that β-lactams cannot bind. Every β-lactam therefore fails. Vancomycin binds peptidoglycan directly and covers most Gram-positives including MRSA, and the lecture's cellulitis case says to consider it when the patient has MRSA risk factors.

  • Cloxacillin: an anti-staphylococcal penicillin, good for MSSA and GAS cellulitis, but it is exactly the drug MRSA resists.
  • Amoxicillin: an aminopenicillin without anti-staphylococcal activity.
  • Carbapenem: the broadest spectrum of all, but the lecture notes it still misses MRSA and VRE.

b4-w14-meds2024-q2-2.html:
From 06 - New Vaccine Platforms and 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. A subunit vaccine uses one component of the pathogen as the antigen rather than the whole organism. The Pfizer vaccine makes the immune system respond to a single protein, the spike, so of these four classes it fits subunit best. It contains no live virus, so it cannot shed or cause a positive PCR test.

  • A: live attenuated vaccines (MMR) contain a weakened, replicating pathogen.
  • B: inactivated whole-cell vaccines (IPV, hepatitis A) contain the entire killed organism.
  • C: toxoids (tetanus, diphtheria) target an inactivated bacterial toxin, and SARS-CoV-2 is a virus.

flags.title: The lecture treats mRNA as its own platform
flags.html: 06 - New Vaccine Platforms lists RNA vaccines as a next-generation platform, separate from the traditional protein subunit vaccines (Novavax, seasonal influenza), whose protein is made in bacteria and injected. “Subunit” is only the best of the four options offered. If “mRNA vaccine” is an option, choose it.

b4-w14-meds2024-q20-20:
From 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 2 and 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. E. coli is an aerobic Gram-negative bacillus. Metronidazole (Flagyl) is the anaerobe drug on the spectrum map. In the peritonitis case it is added to ceftriaxone precisely because ceftriaxone lacks anaerobic cover, and it does nothing for an aerobic E. coli UTI.

  • Aminoglycosides: on the map for Gram-negatives.
  • Amoxicillin: has Gram-negative activity against susceptible E. coli. The cystitis case says to check prior susceptibility reports because of resistance such as ESBLs.
  • Meropenem and piperacillin-tazobactam: both cover E. coli, but they are broader than needed, so they are appropriate yet not first choice.
b4-w14-meds2024-q23-23:
From 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. Enzymatic degradation means the bacterium makes an enzyme that destroys the drug. ESBL (extended-spectrum β-lactamase) inactivates most β-lactams except carbapenems, and ESBL E. coli is the lecture's example. This is a major resistance mechanism in Gram-negatives, and the ESBL gene is often acquired on a plasmid.

  • A: D-Ala-D-Ala → D-Ala-D-Lac is target alteration (VRE). The drug stays intact but cannot bind.
  • C: porin mutation restricts entry (Klebsiella, Pseudomonas).
  • D: efflux pumps remove the drug (P. aeruginosa).
b4-w14-meds2024-q24-24:
From 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. Efflux pumps actively move antibiotic back out of the bacterial cell. This is one arm of “preventing antibiotic accumulation”, whose net effect is lower intracellular drug levels. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the lecture's example.

  • C: porin mutation belongs to the same family but works by decreasing entry through the outer membrane, not by removing drug already inside.
  • A: target alteration (D-Ala-D-Lac in VRE), so the drug cannot bind.
  • B: ESBL destroys the drug enzymatically.
b4-w14-meds2024-q25-25:
From 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. Vancomycin works by binding the D-Ala-D-Ala end of the peptidoglycan precursor and blocking cell-wall cross-linking. Vancomycin-resistant enterococci change that terminus to D-Ala-D-Lac, a structural change to the binding site itself (“altered target”), so the drug can no longer interfere with wall synthesis.

  • B: ESBL is enzymatic degradation of the drug, not a change in the wall target.
  • C: porin mutation restricts entry.
  • D: efflux pumps remove the drug.

B, C and D all lower the drug available at its target. Only A alters the target structure.

b4-w14-meds2024-q3-3.html:
From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines (Block 1). Both are non-live subunit vaccines. A polysaccharide vaccine uses capsular sugar alone and is not immunogenic in children under 2. A conjugate joins that polysaccharide to a protein, which gives a T-cell-dependent response, so it is more immunogenic and can be given at all ages (Prevnar 13, Hib, meningococcal). The lecture records no added danger: as non-live vaccines, both cannot replicate or cause disease.

  • A matches the lecture: more immunogenic, and just as safe.
  • B adds a safety penalty the lecture never states.
  • C is backwards: the conjugate contains the polysaccharide.
  • D: conjugates are non-live, not live attenuated.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The bank keys B (“more immunogenic but slightly more dangerous”). 09 - Introduction to Vaccines says conjugates are more immunogenic and usable at every age. It lists non-live vaccines as safe because they cannot replicate or cause disease, and says nothing about conjugates being riskier. The material supports A. Check the source key before relying on B.

b4-w14-meds2024-q31-31:
From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Endemic means the constant presence of a disease in a population, or its usual prevalence there. A TB rate that has stayed persistently high on reserves for years, driven by lasting structural conditions (overcrowding, poor ventilation, food insecurity), is an endemic pattern, however unacceptable the level is.

  • Sporadic: infrequent and irregular cases (e.g. SARS-CoV-1), each acted on rapidly.
  • Epidemic: a rise above what is expected (e.g. the influenza spike each winter). A chronic baseline is not a rise above itself.
  • Pandemic: an epidemic spread across countries or continents.
b4-w14-meds2024-q32-32:
From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Isolation separates sick people with a contagious disease from those who are not sick, and it lasts for the period of communicability. Quarantine restricts the movement of people who were exposed, to see whether they become sick, and it lasts for the incubation period. Taylor is a confirmed, symptomatic case, so she isolates. Drake is an asymptomatic close contact, so he quarantines. SARS-CoV-2 is communicable from 48 h before symptoms, and its incubation is 2-14 days.

  • A swaps the two terms.
  • C treats a confirmed case as merely exposed.
  • D treats an exposed contact as a case.
  • E is the distractor.

b4-w14-meds2024-q33-33.html:
From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Every option except propagated is a common-source outbreak, so the discriminator is how long exposure lasted. In a point source, exposure is brief and all cases fall within one incubation period, giving a sharp rise and fall. A continuous source exposes cases to the same source over an extended period, which flattens and widens the curve. An intermittent source produces repeated small spikes from on-off exposure (Legionella biofilms). A propagated outbreak spreads person to person, with no single source.

The stem says the hedgehogs could not be removed until enough data had been gathered, so exposure went on for as long as it took to implicate them. That describes a continuous common source, not a brief point exposure.

flags.title: The epidemic curve is missing
flags.html: The stem says “the epidemic curve is shown below”, but the bank has no image. The question was meant to be answered from the curve's shape.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The bank keys A (point common-source). 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation defines a point source as exposure over a brief period, with cases within one incubation period. A source that stayed in place until epidemiologic data implicated it is ongoing exposure, which the lecture calls continuous common-source (B). The missing curve may have shown a single sharp peak, but the text as written supports B.

b4-w14-meds2024-q34-34:
From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Both measures exist to stop spread, and neither treats symptoms. Isolation separates sick people with a contagious disease from people who are not sick, for the period of communicability, so it is the measure for someone who has developed COVID-19. Quarantine restricts people who were exposed, for the incubation period, to see whether they become sick.

  • A: quarantine is for exposed people, not affected ones. The statement describes isolation.
  • B, D: neither measure is a treatment, and neither reduces symptoms.

b4-w14-meds2024-q35-35.html:
From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Check each statement against the lecture's four curve patterns.

  • A false: a continuous common source means cases exposed to the same source over an extended period, a property of the exposure, not a verdict that control measures failed.
  • B true: a point source is a single brief exposure, like one contaminated meal, with all cases within one incubation period.
  • C true: a propagated outbreak spreads person to person. Each generation of cases arrives about one incubation period after the last, so the curve shows successive peaks. The lecture names the person-to-person mechanism, not the peak spacing.
  • D (keyed true): the lecture defines intermittent common source as intermittent spikes from intermittent exposures to one source (e.g. Legionella). A curve that mixes continuous and propagated transmission describes a mixed outbreak.

flags.title: The key looks wrong for D
flags.html: The bank keys B, C and D. 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation describes an intermittent common-source outbreak as repeated small spikes from on-off exposure to a single source, with no propagated component. A curve that combines continuous-source and propagated transmission is a mixed outbreak, which the lecture does not call intermittent. On the lecture's definitions the supported answer is B, C.

b4-w14-meds2024-q36-36:
From 09 - Antivirals. CMV needs the ganciclovir family: ganciclovir and valganciclovir cover CMV, while acyclovir and valacyclovir cover only HSV-1, HSV-2 and VZV. Ganciclovir is IV only. Valganciclovir is its oral prodrug (bioavailability 55%), so it is the answer for a patient who wants a tablet.

  • A acyclovir and B valacyclovir: both oral options exist, but neither covers CMV.
  • C ganciclovir: right spectrum, wrong route (IV).
b4-w14-meds2024-q37-37:
From 09 - Antivirals. Neuraminidase frees newly formed influenza particles from the cell surface as they bud off. Neuraminidase inhibitors, oseltamivir (oral) and zanamivir (inhaled), therefore prevent budding and release.

  • Acyclovir: a guanosine analogue that inhibits herpesvirus DNA polymerase. It has no influenza activity.
  • Baloxavir marboxil: an influenza drug, but it is a cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor that blocks RNA replication, an earlier step.
  • Foscarnet: a pyrophosphate analogue that inhibits viral DNA polymerase, used for drug-resistant herpesviruses and CMV.
b4-w14-meds2024-q38-38:
From 09 - Antivirals. Spectrum is the dividing line. Ganciclovir covers CMV (plus HSV and VZV), while valacyclovir, like acyclovir, covers HSV-1, HSV-2 and VZV and not CMV.

  • A: both need activation. The lecture says these guanosine analogues are prodrugs that must be triphosphorylated, starting with viral thymidine kinase. Valacyclovir is additionally an oral prodrug of acyclovir.
  • B: ganciclovir and its prodrug valganciclovir share the same virus-specific activation, so both are selective.
  • C: valacyclovir treats HSV-1 and HSV-2, and the lecture recommends acyclovir or valacyclovir for them.
  • E: foscarnet and acyclovir both inhibit viral DNA polymerase, by different chemistry.
b4-w14-meds2024-q39-39:
From 09 - Antivirals. Acyclovir must be triphosphorylated before it can act on viral DNA polymerase, and the first phosphorylation is done by viral thymidine kinase. That enzyme is absent from uninfected cells, which is why the drug is inactive in normal cells and selective for infected ones.

  • A: hemagglutinin mediates attachment. Blocking virion release is what the neuraminidase inhibitors do.
  • C: foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analogue that inhibits viral DNA polymerase, not envelope binding.
  • D is backwards: ganciclovir is IV only, and oral valganciclovir is the prodrug designed to give 55% bioavailability.
b4-w14-meds2024-q6-6:
From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines (Block 1). The lecture's PrEP table gives each disease's pre-exposure options.

  • Measles: IG is N/A, so the only pre-exposure option is vaccine, given 2 weeks before.
  • Varicella: IG is N/A, so the only option is vaccine, given 4-6 weeks before. The lecture stresses there is no chemo- or immuno-PrEP for varicella.
  • Hepatitis A: has both options. IG 2 weeks before suits immunocompromised people, infants under 6 months, chronic liver disease or age over 40, and vaccine suits travellers 6 months or older.

So only i and ii are vaccine-only, which is A. B, C and D each include hepatitis A.

b4-w14-new-q10-10.html:
From 06 - New Vaccine Platforms. Viral-vector vaccines (adenovirus, as in Janssen and AstraZeneca) carry a named disadvantage: patients can mount a strong immune reaction to the vector itself, especially if previously exposed, with lower efficacy. That is why repeated dosing may lose effect.

  • A lipid nanoparticles are how mRNA vaccines are delivered.
  • C the cold chain is the mRNA drawback; viral vectors are stable in regular storage.
  • B the bank assigns this to mRNA (rare myocarditis/pericarditis); see the note below.

flags.title: Option B is arguable
flags.html: 06 - New Vaccine Platforms lists a strong immune reaction to the vector as a viral-vector disadvantage, and VITT as its rare side effect, so “triggers unintended immune reactions” could describe adenoviral vectors too. D is the more specific match; the key's claim that B belongs only to mRNA is not in the note.

b4-w14-new-q18-18:
From 09 - Antivirals. Neuraminidase frees newly budded virions from the cell surface, so the neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir) stop viral particles leaving the host cell. The lecture also stresses that compared with placebo they shorten symptoms by only about 1 day, a modest effect.

  • A true (release step of the life cycle).
  • C true.
  • B false: oseltamivir is right, but “zyclovir” is not a drug (acyclovir, the look-alike, is a herpesvirus drug).
  • D fails because it includes B.

b4-w14-new-q2-2.html:
From 01 - Transmission of Infectious Agents. The lecture's examples by mode:

  • I C. difficile: direct contact, listed with MRSA as the most common mode.
  • II varicella zoster: airborne (particles under 5 microns, with TB and measles).
  • III Plasmodium falciparum: vector-borne (mosquito), like West Nile and dengue.
  • IV C. botulinum: common vehicle, the lecture's example being home-canned food.

So the four agents map to four different modes; none of them share a mode.

flags.title: An option was lost in transcription
flags.html: The “C.” of C. difficile was read as option letter C, so the real option C is missing and item I's name is broken. The surviving options are A airborne, B vector, D direct contact.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives C for both I (C. difficile) and IV (C. botulinum). 01 - Transmission of Infectious Agents puts C. difficile under direct contact and botulism under common vehicle, so the two cannot share a letter. Whatever the lost option C was, one of those two keyed pairs contradicts the lecture; on the surviving options I should be D (direct contact).

b4-w14-new-q20-20:
From 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. Every statement is in the lecture:

  • A enzymatic inactivation by β-lactamase is called a major resistance mechanism for Gram-negative pathogens.
  • B β-lactamases destroy drugs containing the β-lactam ring (penicillins, cephalosporins).
  • C they can be plasmid-borne (ESBL is picked up on a plasmid, per Lecture 1) or chromosomal.
  • D the SPACE organisms (Serratia, Pseudomonas/Proteus, Acinetobacter, Citrobacter, Enterobacter) carry AmpC β-lactamases encoded on their chromosomes.

With all four true, E is the only complete answer.
b4-w14-new-q21-21:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. The lecture names qSOFA as the bedside score for recognising sepsis, reserving the full SOFA score for measuring organ failure in trials.

  • A septic shock is hypotension that does not respond to fluids, not one that responds half the time.
  • B sepsis follows infection by bacteria, viruses or fungi.
  • C cardiovascular dysfunction means low BP with a high heart rate and weak contraction, not a falling heart rate.
  • E source control is one of the four management principles: you must find and control the cause (drain, operate, remove the device).
b4-w14-new-q3-3:
From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. The lecture groups antibiotics by the bacterial process they hit:

  • I β-lactams → B: bind penicillin-binding proteins and block peptidoglycan cross-linking (cell wall).
  • II macrolides → C: bind the 50S subunit (protein synthesis).
  • III quinolones → D: inhibit DNA gyrase, a type II topoisomerase (nucleic acid synthesis).
  • IV aminoglycosides → C: bind 30S and cause mRNA misreading (protein synthesis).
  • V carbapenems → B: they are β-lactams, the broadest-spectrum ones (cell wall).
  • VI sulfonamides → A: folate synthesis inhibitors (e.g. TMP-SMX).
b4-w14-new-q9-9:
From 16 - How Viruses Work. The lecture's table on SARS-CoV-2 and influenza as multisystem disease lists, for SARS-CoV-2:

  • A respiratory: respiratory failure (ARDS).
  • B VTE: PE and DVT, with stroke listed under CNS.
  • C cardiac: acute cardiac injury and arrhythmias.

It also adds GI upset, anosmia, headache and a Kawasaki-like cytokine storm. Because all three options appear, E (all of the above) beats D (A and B only), which leaves out the cardiac injury.

b4-w14-sa-q2-2.html:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. What separates severe sepsis from sepsis is organ dysfunction. The lecture's early-recognition physiology lists the kidney sign as oliguria, and acute kidney injury is one of the organ failures of MODS, so low urine output is evidence that an organ is failing.

  • A, C fever and tachycardia are signs of the systemic inflammatory response that sepsis already has; on their own they show no organ failure.
  • B recent surgery is a high-risk group for sepsis, not a feature of its severity.
  • E shortness of breath is a symptom; the lung dysfunction the lecture counts is hypoxia or ARDS, which the option does not establish.

flags.title: The case was not banked with this question
flags.html: “This patient” refers to a shared self-assessment case that is not in the stem, most likely the bowel perforation during colonoscopy in the preceding question (b4-w14-sa-q1-1). The reasoning here does not depend on its details.

b4-w14-sa-q3-3.html:
From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. Cell wall agents are the β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) and the glycopeptides (vancomycin). Imipenem (carbapenem), cefazolin (1st-gen cephalosporin) and amoxicillin (aminopenicillin) are all β-lactams.

  • A ciprofloxacin inhibits DNA gyrase.
  • B clindamycin binds 50S and gentamicin binds 30S (protein synthesis).
  • D doxycycline (30S) and clarithromycin (50S) are protein synthesis inhibitors; only vancomycin fits.
  • E clindamycin is a lincosamide acting on 50S, although imipenem and amoxicillin-clavulanate are β-lactams.

b4-w14-sa-q6-6:
From 02 and 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely. Gram-positive cocci in clusters are staphylococci, so S. aureus bacteremia is the worry. Injection drug use is on the lecture list of MRSA risk factors (09 - Approach to a Patient with Fever), and a febrile bacteremic patient is in the sepsis/deep-seated column, where the IV choice with MRSA risk is vancomycin. Empirically you assume the worst until susceptibilities return.

  • A piperacillin-tazobactam is broad Gram-negative/anti-pseudomonal cover that the lecture does not use for MRSA.
  • B cefazolin treats MSSA but not MRSA; it is where you narrow to once the isolate proves susceptible.
  • C ciprofloxacin is weak against Gram-positives.
  • E clindamycin is a bacteriostatic oral option for stable MRSA-risk SSTI, not empiric bacteremia therapy.
b4-w15-meds2024-q27-27:
From 03 - Important Fungal Infections. The lecture makes the exception explicit: tinea versicolour is NOT a dermatophyte infection; it is caused by Malassezia furfur. The other “tinea” conditions (capitis, corporis, cruris, pedis, unguium) are dermatophyte infections.

  • A Candida causes mucocutaneous thrush, vulvovaginal and diaper candidiasis, not pigmented patches.
  • B Saccharomyces cerevisiae is baker's yeast and is not a pathogen in the lecture.
  • D Aspergillus is an invasive or allergic mould of the lungs and sinuses.
  • E tinea corporis is a disease name (a dermatophyte infection of the body), not an organism.

b4-w15-new-q19-19.html:
From 03 - Important Fungal Infections. The lecture gives this exact description for mucormycosis: on calcofluor white stain of tissue or BAL, wide, irregular hyphae (6–15 μm) with few septations that twist like a ribbon and branch at 90°. Transplant recipients are a named risk group. So the stain points to C.

  • A, B Candida and Cryptococcus are yeasts; they bud rather than forming wide hyphae (Cryptococcus is diagnosed by CrAg).
  • D dermatophytes are superficial moulds of hair, skin and nails and do not cause pneumonia.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The bank keys D (dermatophytes). 03 - Important Fungal Infections describes wide, irregular hyphae with few septations on calcofluor white of BAL as the hallmark of mucormycosis (C), lists transplantation as a risk factor, and places dermatophytes among the superficial mycoses of hair, skin and nails. The lecture supports C.

b4-w15-new-q24-24.html:
From 04 - Antifungals. Azoles inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (a CYP450), so no ergosterol is made and the membrane's permeability is altered. That is the one correct pairing.

  • C echinocandins inhibit 1,3-β-D-glucan synthesis in the cell wall; they leave ergosterol alone.
  • D amphotericin B (a polyene) binds ergosterol and inserts into the membrane, forming pores; the glucan target belongs to the echinocandins. C and D have swapped mechanisms.
  • A the allylamines are not in the lecture; see the note below.

flags.title: Option A is not covered by the notes
flags.html: Neither 03 - Important Fungal Infections nor 04 - Antifungals covers allylamines (terbinafine). In general pharmacology they inhibit squalene epoxidase, an earlier step in ergosterol synthesis, so “disrupts the fungal cell membrane” is at best imprecise. Verify it before relying on it.

b4-w15-new-q3-3.html:
From 05 - Approach to Immunodeficiency. Secondary immunodeficiency is the most common type in practice. The lecture's causes are malignancy (lymphoma, leukemia), immunosuppressive drugs, chronic infection such as HIV, asplenia, malnutrition, prematurity or older age, and environmental stress.

  • A and C are both named, so E (A, C) is the keyed answer.
  • B iron deficiency is not listed on its own; the nearest cause in the lecture is general malnutrition, and the question's author has excluded it.

Asplenia does not stop immune cells being made; it removes the spleen's filtering of encapsulated bacteria.

flags.title: An option was lost in transcription
flags.html: The options run A, B, C, E: option D is missing, and the answer is a free-text sentence rather than a letter. The key's reason (“damage the body's ability to produce immune cells”) fits malignancy but not asplenia.

b4-w15-new-q5-5.html:
From 06 - Approach to Allergy. Of patients labelled penicillin-allergic, more than 90% are not allergic on skin testing, and the lecture lists why:

  • A the reaction was often an intolerance (diarrhea, nausea), not an allergy.
  • C labelled patients are more likely to get alternative broad-spectrum antibiotics, with more C. difficile, MRSA and surgical site infection from less perioperative cefazolin.
  • D the most common cause of a rash is the infection, not the drug.

Every statement is supported, which is what the bank's own rationale says (“all of the options describe a penicillin allergy”).

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The bank keys D, but its own rationale says all of the options are true, and 06 - Approach to Allergy supports A, C and D each in turn (intolerance, the switch to broad-spectrum alternatives, infection as the usual cause of rash). On the lecture the answer is E (all of the above).

flags.title: An option was lost in transcription
